utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-69-A, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now may I have the appearances of the parties, beginning with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. Michelle Jarvis, appearing for the Prosecution today, together with Mr. Mathias Marcussen, Ms. Barbara Goy, Ms. Grace Harbour, and our Case Manager, Mr. Colin Nawrot. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now before asking for appearances for the Defence, I note for the record that pursuant to the terms of the Scheduling Order for the appeal hearing issued by the Appeals Chamber on 12th June 2015, Mr. Simatovic has filed a notification on 19 June 2015 indicating that he will not exercise his right to be present during this hearing. Mr. Stanisic has also informally informed the Chamber, through e-mail correspondence on 1st July 2015, that he will not attend this hearing. Now, may I have the appearances for the counsel for Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning. Myself, Wayne Jordash, Scott Martin, Ms. Bracq, Ms. Marchand, Mr. Parker, Mr. Crowe. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: And now for counsel for Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Vladimir Petrovic, attorney-at-law, and I represent the Defence of Franko Simatovic today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. This case concerns the events that took place between April 1991 and 31st December 1995 in Serbian Autonomous Area of Krajina, the SAO Krajina, the Serbian Autonomous Area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem in Croatia, as well as in the municipalities of Bijeljina, Bosanski Samac, Doboj, Sanski Most, Trnovo, and Zvornik in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic were charged with committing murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war, and murder, deportation, other inhumane acts (forcible transfer), and persecution as crimes against humanity in the context of these events. The Prosecution charged the accused with committing these crimes pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Tribunal's Statute, through participation in the joint criminal enterprise, the alleged common criminal purpose of which was the forcible and permanent removal of the majority of the non-Serbs from large areas of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In addition, Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic were charged pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Tribunal's Statute with having planned, ordered, and/or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation and/or execution of the crimes alleged in the indictment. On 30 May 2013, Trial Chamber I of the Tribunal rendered its judgement. The Trial Chamber found that many of the crimes alleged in the indictment were perpetrated by various Serb forces in the mentioned locality in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, the Trial Chamber, Judge Picard dissenting, found that neither Stanisic nor Simatovic were responsible for committing these crimes pursuant to JCE liability, as it was not established beyond a reasonable doubt that they possessed the requisite mens rea for JCE liability. The Trial Chamber also found that it was not proven beyond a reasonable doubt that either Mr. Stanisic or Mr. Simatovic planned or ordered these crimes. Further, the Trial Chamber, Judge Picard dissenting, found that neither Mr. Stanisic nor Mr. Simatovic were responsible for aiding and abetting these crimes as the actus reus elements of aiding and abetting liability were not established beyond a reasonable doubt. Consequently, the Trial Chamber, Judge Picard dissenting, found that Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic were not guilty of any count in the indictment. The Prosecution challenges the trial Judgement on three grounds. Under its first ground of appeal, the Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber erred in law and in fact in finding that the mens rea of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic for JCE liability was not established. The Prosecution requests that the Appeals Chamber: (a) overturn the acquittals of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic; (b) apply the correct legal standards to the evidence and find that all elements of JCE liability are established, taking into account their acts and omissions as found by the Trial Chamber and as set out in its ground of appeal; (c) convict Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute based on their participation in the JCE alleged in the indictment for the crimes listed under Counts 1 through 5; and (d) sentence them accordingly. Under its second ground of appeal, the Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber erred in law and in fact in finding that the actus reus of aiding and abetting liability was not established with respect to the conduct of either Mr. Stanisic or Mr. Simatovic in relation to the crimes committed in the municipalities of Bosanski Samac, in Doboj, as well as in the SAO Krajina. The Prosecutor requests that the Appeals Chamber: (1) overturn the acquittals of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic; (2) apply the correct standard to the evidence and find that all elements of aiding and abetting liability are established, taking into account their acts and omissions as found by the Trial Chamber and as set out in its third ground of appeal; (3) convict Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute for aiding and abetting the crimes listed under grounds 1 through 5; and, (4), sentence them accordingly. Alternatively, with respect to both its first and second grounds of appeal, the Prosecution requests that the Appeals Chamber find the alleged errors established and, I quote, "remand the case to a Bench of the Tribunal" to apply the correct legal standards to the trial record and to determine the liability of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic as alleged in the indictment. Under its third ground of appeal in part, the Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber erred in fact in failing to find that Mr. Stanisic significantly contributed to the implementation of the common criminal purpose of the JCE in the SAO SBWS and in the municipalities of Bijeljina and Zvornik, and that both Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic significantly contributed to the implementation of the common criminal purpose of the JCE in the municipality of Sanski Most. The Prosecution requests that the Appeals Chamber: (1) apply the correct legal standard to the evidence and find that Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic made their respective significant contributions as alleged; (2) take these findings into account in convicting Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic for their participation in the JCE under its first ground of appeal; and, (3), sentence them accordingly. Further, under the remaining part of its third ground of appeal, the Prosecution argues, in the alternative, that the Trial Chamber erred in fact in failing to find that Mr. Stanisic substantially contributed to one or more of the crimes committed in the SAO SBWS and in the municipalities of Bijeljina and Zvornik; that both Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic substantially contributed to one or more of the crimes committed in the municipality of Sanski Most, and that they therefore aided and abetted these crimes. The Prosecution requests that the Appeals Chamber: (1) apply the correct legal standard to the evidence and find that Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic made their respective substantial contributions as alleged; (2) takes these findings into account in convicting Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic as aiders and abettors under its second ground of appeal; and, (3), sentence them accordingly. Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic respond that the Prosecution's appeal should be dismissed in its entirety and that any conviction in appeal would violate their fair trial right to have their conviction reviewed. Additionally, Mr. Simatovic submits that in the event that the Appeals Chamber grants the Prosecution appeal, it should return the case to a Bench of the Tribunal. Now, let me turn to the manner in which we will conduct this hearing today. I would like to recall that an appeal is not a trial de novo and the parties must refrain from repeating their case as presented at trial. Arguments must be limited to alleged errors of law which invalidate the trial judgement or alleged errors of fact which occasion a miscarriage of justice. Throughout the hearing, counsel may argue the ground of appeal in any order they consider suitable for their presentations; however, I would urge counsel to not repeat verbatim or summarise extensively the arguments presented in their briefs. The Appeals Chamber is familiar with the briefs. Furthermore, the parties are requested to provide precise references to materials supporting their oral arguments. The Judges, of course, will interrupt the parties at any time to ask questions or they may ask questions following each party's submissions or at the end of the hearing. I would like to remind the parties to be particularly careful not to reveal any information that could identify a protected witness or other protected information. Finally, I bring to your attention the timetable outlined in the order amending the Scheduling Order for the appeal hearing issued on 30 June 2015. The hearing will proceed as follows: First, we will hear submissions from the Prosecution for one hour and 30 minutes. Following a pause for lunch of an hour and 20 minutes, counsel for Mr. Stanisic, and then counsel for Mr. Simatovic will present their response. And, at the end, the Prosecution will have 30 minutes to reply. Now, I would like to invite the Prosecution to present its submissions. You have one hour and 30 minutes for that. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and Your Honours. The Prosecution has taken the serious step of appealing the acquittals of the accused because the trial judgement contains serious errors. These errors have blocked justice and accountability in this case, and if followed in the future, have the potential to derail international criminal law in some alarming ways. At the heart of the problem is a fundamental failure by the majority Judges to adjudicate the essential issues before them. The accused were alleged to be members of a joint criminal enterprise where the common purpose was to remove the majority of the non-Serb population from large parts of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina between 1991 and 1995. In other words, an ethnic cleansing joint criminal enterprise. But the evidence of this common criminal purpose which was adduced by the Prosecution at trial is missing from the majority's analysis; and, in particular, from its assessment of the accused's shared intent. In this joint criminal enterprise case, the judgement contains no findings on whether there was a common criminal purpose, and, if so, its nature and duration, who the JCE members were, or the units or structures they used to implement their purpose. Without looking at the accused's intent through the lens of this common criminal purpose, and most importantly through the lens of what the accused knew about that common criminal purpose, the majority has deprived itself of the essential compass it needed to guide the conclusions that it reached. I'll begin our submissions today, Your Honours, by explaining in a nutshell the serious problem with the Trial Chamber's methodology in this case and the outcome reached and why it is so important for Your Honours to correct it. Mr. Marcussen will then address you in more detail on ground 1 of our appeal concerning the joint criminal enterprise. He'll explain how, notwithstanding some passing references to the common criminal purpose in abstract, the majority's failure to apply the common criminal purpose lens throughout its analysis of shared intent led the majority into error. He'll show that if they had not erred, they would have considered the evidence of the pattern of crimes, the intent of the other JCE members and, most importantly, what the accused knew about the common purpose. He'll show that had the majority assessed the accused's continuing contributions in light of their knowledge of the common criminal purpose, the inference of shared intent is inescapable. Regarding ground 2, our alternative argument on aiding and abetting, we'll primarily rely on the arguments that we set out in our appeal brief. I would just add that we now, of course, know that the aiding and abetting acquittals in this case have been tainted by the rejected specific direction requirement. As the Appeals Chamber has subsequently confirmed in Sainovic, appeal judgement, paragraph 1649, and confirmed in the Popovic appeal judgement more recently at appeal judgement paragraph 1758, specific direction does not form part of the elements of aiding and abetting under customary international law. Regarding ground 3 of our appeal, we will primarily rely on the arguments in our brief and won't make further submissions on that today. After Mr. Marcussen's submissions in relation to ground 1, I'll conclude by addressing Your Honours on the question of remedy. If Your Honours agree with us that the problems in this judgement must be fixed, what can most fairly and appropriately be done? But to begin, Your Honours, what is so wrong with the majority judgement in this case that we have taken this serious step of appealing the acquittals? Your Honours, this case goes to the very heart of the ethnic cleansing campaign unleashed against the non-Serb populations of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina between 1991 and 1995. It raised for adjudication fundamental issues about how the ethnic cleansing was carried out, who was behind it and, most importantly, of course, the role that the two accused in this case played in it. Satisfactory answers to these questions are entirely missing from the judgement. The evidence showed that these two influential and well-informed individuals - Stanisic, as chief of the Serbian security service, and Simatovic as his trusted right-hand man - were deeply involved in the machinery through which this massive ethnic cleansing campaign was carried out. They were everywhere. They created, trained, funded, armed, supported, assisted, or were otherwise linked to many of the formations that were integral to the ethnic cleansing process, including some of the most notorious groups like Arkan's Tigers, otherwise known as the SDG, and indeed their own unit, the Red Berets. The evidence showed that the accused were involved with the formations committing the crimes, first in Croatia - in the Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina and the Serb Autonomous Region in eastern Croatia called SAO SBWS - and then in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This involvement closely tracked the hotspots of the ethnic cleansing activity as the campaign unfolded over more than four years. In Krajina, they trained personnel who then engaged in ethnic cleansing. Knowing of these crimes, they then exported the same training model to the SAO SBWS and Bosnia-Herzegovina where a similar pattern of ethnic cleansing unfolded. They knew of the ethnic cleansing agenda of the people they acted with: Martic, Babic, Hadzic, Karadzic, Mladic, Milosevic, Arkan. They knew of the crimes systemically committed across all three regions in pursuit of this goal and continued to assist anyway again and again and again. Why then did the majority consider that the accused were not responsible as JCE members?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: In our appeal brief, we have identified multiple legal and factual errors. These include the Trial Chamber's obviously compartmentalised assessment which has obscured the coherence of the circumstantial evidence adduced by the Prosecution. We maintain our arguments on all the errors set out in our brief. But today, Your Honours, I want to focus on the majority Judges' failure to apply the common criminal purpose lens in assessing the shared intent of the accused. The entire verdict in this JCE case hinges on the majority Judges' inference that the accused might simply have intended lawful military activity; that it was reasonably possible they only sought to assist in establishing lawful Serb territorial control. We see that, Your Honours, for example, in the trial judgement at paragraphs 2326, 2330, 2332, and 2334. But that is a conclusion they could not have reached if they had analysed the contributions and the statements of the accused through the lens of the common criminal purpose. By looking at the events in abstract, the Chamber constructed a situation where the goal of territorial control could be separated from the crimes committed. But the objective of the Serb forces, their common purpose, was never limited to taking control of territory by lawful means. It was about taking and maintaining control of Serb-claimed territory by ethnically cleansing the non-Serb populations living there. The Serb leadership intended to take and maintain control of the land they coveted for their Serb state inhabited, as it was, by large numbers of non-Serbs by permanently changing the demographics. The JCE members intended fundamental ethnic recomposition of the population to ensure the overwhelming Serbian majorities they needed to guarantee continued control. And to do that, everyone involved must have known the crimes of forcible transfer, deportation, and other violent crimes would be needed to terrify or otherwise force the non-Serb population out. No one involved over and over again in the territorial control operations, which entailed massive expulsions and other violent crimes, could possibly have intended only lawful military activity. That is simply divorced from reality, Your Honours. Certainly, if it really were the case that these accused only intended lawful military activity and did not intend the ethnic cleansing component of the equation of territorial control, we would expect to see the accused repudiating the crimes and the displacement of the non-Serb population. Instead, we see their continued support for the implementation of the common criminal purpose over a period of years through their contributions to the Serb forces committing crimes. The failure to apply the common criminal purpose lens is starkly revealed in the majority's finding that the accused were only aware of a risk of crimes happening in the course of territorial control or that crimes were only reasonably foreseeable to the accused. We see that, for example, in the trial judgement at paragraphs 2323, 2332, and 2333. But, Your Honours, the very nature of the common criminal purpose made crimes a certainty, not a risk. To illustrate the impact of the majority's missing common purpose lens, let me give you a simplified hypothetical example. The accused drives two armed men to a bank and drops them off. The accused's conduct in driving the car, of course, is not inherently unlawful. But if you apply the majority's approach, you would conclude that the accused might know of a risk of crimes, a risk that these armed men would rob the bank, but the majority would allow for the reasonable possibility that the accused might only have intended the lawful purpose of transporting them to a bank and therefore didn't share the intent to commit the armed robbery. But if we add in evidence that the accused knew the common -- the purpose of the trip to the bank was an armed robbery, the inferences about the accused's intent are entirely different. And certainly, Your Honours, if the accused drove the men, the armed men, to multiple banks over the course of the next year knowing that they had committed armed robbery on previous occasions, the conclusion would be inescapable that the accused was acting jointly and intended the crimes. It's only by failing to look at the situation through the lens of the common purpose that you could ever reach the conclusion the accused might only have intended lawful purposes. Which brings me to the key problem with the majority's intent analysis. Not only did the majority fail to adjudicate the existence of the common criminal purpose, it then failed to consider in its shared intent analysis whether the accused knew about that common criminal purpose, whether the accused knew that taking over and maintaining control of Serb territory in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina inherently involved the commission of the crimes required to expel the population. That was a fundamental issue that had to be adjudicated in determining the charged crimes. The accused's awareness that territorial control inherently entailed the commission of crimes coupled with their repeated contributions to the common purpose provides a compelling foundation for inferring shared intent and one that was ignored completely in the majority's analysis. In sum, Your Honours, essential questions, essential issues in this case about the common criminal purpose, the accused's knowledge of that purpose, and the resulting impact on the assessment of their shared intent have not been considered or resolved. That is why we say there is a legal error of failure to adjudicate or failure to provide a reasoned opinion. I refer Your Honours, for example, to the Kvocka appeal judgement, paragraph 23, emphasizing that a Trial Chamber is required to make "findings of those facts which are essential to the determination of guilt on a particular count," and that failure to do so is a legal error. Also the Gotovina appeal judgement, at paragraph 12, confirming that a lack of a reasoned opinion can arise from a failure to address "relevant issues, factual findings or arguments." The majority's failure to ask itself these essential questions led it to miss crucial pieces of evidence compounding its legal error in failing to provide a reasoned opinion, and I refer you to Perisic appeal judgement, paragraph 96, in that regard. For example, as Mr. Marcussen will further explain, the majority makes no reference to the pattern of crimes across Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina in its analysis of shared intent or to how actions of the accused and the formations they directed or assisted fit within that pattern of crimes and supported it. It failed to address essential evidence about the intention of the JCE members that show their purpose was to maintain control of seized territories through ethnic cleansing. Your Honours, there are two main reasons why it is so important that the errors in the majority's judgement be corrected. First, to safe-guard the future direction of international criminal law. This case sets many problematic precedents but let me highlight two of the most glaring. If the majority's approach were followed in the future, it would undermine the framework for JCE liability. One of the essential features of JCE is that conduct, which may look lawful when viewed in isolation, is exposed as criminally culpable when viewed in context and its true purpose in propelling a criminal scheme is revealed. In my bank robbery hypothetical, it's about looking at the seemingly lawful act of driving to the bank in its proper context as a contribution towards a plan to commit a bank robbery. The JCE doctrine is important due to the very nature of crimes committed most commonly in wartime situations, which of course very often involve these sorts of vast criminal schemes with multiple actors, many of whom contribute in ways that, viewed in isolation, do not appear criminal. I refer you to the Tadic appeal judgement at paragraph 191 in this regard. But the majority's approach in this case undercuts the very rationale of JCE liability. Instead of looking to see how the contributions of the accused had facilitated the implementation of the common criminal purpose as a whole, the majority focused narrowly on whether there was a direct link between the acts of the accused and specific crimes or criminals. Instead of assessing the role the accused's unit played in furthering the common criminal purpose, the majority focused narrowly on the occasions when the unit members directly committed crimes. In taking this sort of approach, the majority has extended a really significant protective buffer to senior officials. The more senior the position, the more removed their conduct is likely to be from the direct commission of crimes. It's only by stepping back to look at these seemingly neutral acts in context that their role in furthering a criminal purpose is revealed. As Judge Picard said in her dissenting opinion in this case, quoting Judge Jackson: The majority's approach leads to a place where "law has terror only for little men and takes note of only little wrongs." The majority's approach is also problematic for international criminal law because of the implications it has for crimes involving military or combat activity. Again, a scenario frequently arising in international criminal law cases. We accept, of course, Your Honours, that truly lawful military activity in accordance with IHL cannot be rendered unlawful under the framework of international criminal law. But, Your Honours, of course not all military activity is lawful under IHL. In this case, when analysed in the context of all of the evidence about the common criminal purpose, it's clear that the operations to take territorial control were carried out in furtherance of the overarching ethnic cleansing agenda. These operations were directed at non-Serb civilians. The majority has automatically credited anything that looked like it was connected to military matters or combat action as potentially lawful. But in the context of the repeated and systemic pattern of crimes in connection with those military operations, this conclusion is unreasonable. If left uncorrected, this sort of approach would have potentially devastating consequences for international criminal law. But, Your Honours, the most important reason for taking action to correct the errors is to ensure a proper justice process for the victims. Here I'm talking about the serious failure to adjudicate essential issues going to the heart of this case. This has deprived the victims of a meaningful determination of the role that these two accused played in the crimes inflicted on them. The tragedy unleashed by the JCE members in the SAO Krajina, SAO SBWS, and Bosnia-Herzegovina between 1991 and 1995 was immense. As documented just in this case, well over a hundred thousand people were terrorised, uprooted from their homes and communities, and violently expelled. The events devastated dozens of towns and villages all across the self-declared self-Serb republics in the three regions during a period of over four years. The Trial Chamber documented over 270 murders by Serb forces related to the incidents charged. Your Honours, this is not a case where the existing trial judgement can be endorsed. At the very least, the majority's aiding and abetting analysis, tainted by the now rejected specific direction requirement, must be corrected. And while aiding and abetting convictions would provide a measure of justice, they would not most accurately capture the integral role that the two accused played in furthering the vast criminal ethnic cleansing enterprise documented at trial. Your Honours, I now give the floor to Mr. Marcussen to address you further in relation to ground 1 of our appeal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Afande would like to ask a question that goes to Ms. Jarvis, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AFANDE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Prosecutor. I would like to have some clarifications about the parallel that you made between the conduct of armed people robbing a bank and the acts in this case. I'm asking this because I would like to know whether driving people to a bank presupposes that the armed people are criminals on the verge of committing a criminal act, or whether you can drive armed people to a bank without them committing a crime. I don't see the link with this case. Could you be more specific, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Indeed, Your Honour, it would be possible in theory for lawfully armed people to be transported to a bank and leave it at that and not commit a bank robbery. Of course, the fact that the two men in the hypothetical example are armed is enough to give rise to knowledge of a risk of the possibility that, you know, in the circumstances, it's not out of the question that they might be going to the bank to commit a robbery, but it's not a certainty. And I think the example illustrates that if you just look at it in that context, you couldn't understand for certain that a crime would be committed by the two men; although, there are indications in the circumstances that suggest it's a possibility, it's a risk, it's perhaps reasonably foreseeable, and that's exactly the analytical framework that we see in the judgement. We see the majority looking at whether there is anything in the record that might suggest a risk of crimes, and they look at the fact that, well, in some of the operations - Doboj is a good example - the accused knew that the unit had committed crimes very soon prior to that, and so perhaps there was a risk of crimes being committed again in Doboj. That's where we see the impact of the missing common criminal purpose analysis. Because if the Trial Chamber had been really crediting the existence of the common criminal purpose, if they were starting from the proposition that these operations to take territorial control and maintain territorial control were about ethnic cleansing, there is not a risk of crimes happening. There is a certainty of crimes happening. That's the very purpose behind sending the units in, conducting the territorial control operations in order to change the ethnic composition. But, Your Honour, perhaps we can further develop the bank robbery example in a way that might be helpful to you. Suppose that instead of driving the accused to the bank -- sorry, instead of the accused driving the two armed men to the bank, the accused has trained the two armed men in how to use the fire-arms, or the accused has provided the bags to be used to take the cash from the bank. Again, those things, training somebody in the use of a fire-arm, not inherently unlawful. And so if you just look at it in abstract, in isolation, you might not reach the conclusion that the accused intended the bank robbery. But if you add in evidence about the common criminal purpose, about the plan to commit the bank robbery, then obviously the conduct in training the two men in the use of the fire-arms is a contribution towards the armed robbery. And certainly if it happens again and again and again and the accused know that, then the conclusion is inescapable, that there is a common purpose, that they are acting jointly, and the accused indeed intends the commission of the bank robbery. And that's what we say is the situation here, Your Honours. This is a situation where the accused must have known about this common criminal purpose. As Mr. Marcussen will further explain, they were among the most well-informed of people in the three locations as the ethnic cleansing campaign unfolded. They continued to contribute, they continued to equip and build capacity for these territorial control operations, knowing that the crimes were being committed, knowing that that was the purpose behind the territorial control operations, and certainly, when viewed in that context, the conclusion is inescapable, that they indeed intended the crimes. I hope I've assisted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AFANDE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Ms. Jarvis has explained, the Trial Chamber erred in law by failing to adjudicate a central aspect of the Prosecution's case: The existence and nature of the common criminal purpose, and critically the Chamber failed to adjudicate the accused's knowledge of the common criminal purpose. Your Honours, why was it necessary for the Trial Chamber in this case to determine whether a common criminal purpose existed and whether the accused knew that their actions contributed to it when drawing conclusions about their intent? It was necessary because if the accused knew of the existence of the common criminal purpose and repeatedly contributed to its execution, the only reasonable inferences that the accused shared the intent that the crimes of the criminal purpose be committed. But instead of looking at the accused's acts through the lens of a common criminal purpose, the Trial Chamber looked at different segments of the evidence and looked at it in isolation. It looked at the accused's statements without considering the context in which they were made. It looked at the accused's training of Serb forces separately. It looked at their support to Milan Martic and the SAO Krajina police separately. It looked at the crimes of the accused's unit separately. But the majority never looked at the accused's statements and acts together, and it never put them in the context of the pattern of crimes and the common criminal purpose. The Trial Chamber also failed to consider significant evidence that would have required analysis of findings if one were to understand the accused's statements and acts. For example, the Trial Chamber did not consider evidence in the record proving that the strategic objectives of the Bosnian Serbian leadership includes ethnic cleansing of Serb-claimed territory. Nowhere in the judgement is this evidence discussed. The Trial Chamber, therefore, clearly failed to make findings on issues that were central to the determination of the guilt of the accused and its analysis of the evidence was manifestly inadequate. In its shared intent analysis, the majority make reference to the "alleged joint criminal enterprise." Did this mean that the majority, for the purposes of its intent analysis, assumed arguendo the existence of the common criminal purpose? If it did, it would mean that the majority accepted as proven the plan of the Serb leadership was to take and maintain control over Serb-claimed territory in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and ethnically cleanse that territory of the non-Serb population; thus, all the take-over operations in the indictment area was -- inherently involved ethnic cleansing of the non-Serb population. Yet the Chamber concluded that the accused only knew of a risk of crimes, not a certainty of crimes happening, and that the accused might only have intended lawful military activity. There are only two ways that the majority Judges could have reached these conclusions. One possibility is that the majority did not actually fully credit the common criminal purpose because, if it had done that, it would have had to assume that the crimes were an inherent part of the take-overs and therefore it was certain that crimes would be committed. They were not only a risk. The only other way they could have reached these conclusions is finding that the accused did not know of the ethnic cleansing and that it was an inherent part of the take-over operations; in other words, the Trial Chamber would have found that the accused did not know of the common criminal purpose. Either way, it was an error. The majority failed to adjudicate essential issues in the case. If the majority did not actually assume the existence of the common criminal purpose, it would have to make findings on its existence. Yet there are no findings on the common criminal purpose in the judgement. If the majority concluded that the accused did not know of the common criminal purpose, it had to make findings to that effect. However, there are no findings about the accused's knowledge of the common criminal purpose in the judgement. The Trial Chamber, therefore, failed to provide a reasoned opinion. Had the Trial Chamber not erred, it would have found that Stanisic and Simatovic intended the crimes of the JCE based on: (1) the consistent pattern of crimes committed against non-Serbs in each targeted area; (2) the accused's knowledge of both the pattern of crimes and the intent of other JCE members; and, (3), their continued contribution over several years to establishing Serb-dominated ethnically cleansed territories. The only reasonable inference from that is that the accused shared the intent to use crimes to achieve territorial control. First, let's look at the pattern of crimes. The Chamber found that there was a single widespread discriminatory attack on the civilian population across the entire indictment area; at paragraphs 971 and 1251. The findings in volume 1 reveal the attack followed a pattern where it was repeated over and over again in each targeted area. In the SAO Krajina, the non-Serb population fled because of attacks on villages and towns with substantial or complete Croat population. The killings, use of human shields, detention, beating, forced labour, sexual abuse, and other forms of harassment, and the looting and the destruction of property, these crimes were committed by the JNA, the SAO Krajina TO, the SAO Krajina police, including Milan Martic, and Serb parliamentary units, as well as various local Serb authorities; paragraphs 401 and 404. The crimes followed the same pattern in the SAO SBWS. Thousands of non-Serbs fled the area because of the forcible transfer of others, detention, looting, restriction of freedoms, forced labour, beatings, killings, threats, and harassment perpetrated by the same kind of forces, the JNA, Serb volunteers, local authorities, paramilitaries, the SNB, the police, the TO, and Arkan's SDG. You will find this at paragraph 578. And this same pattern was followed in the indictment municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, starting with Bijeljina. So we see this in Bosanski Samac. Numerous people fled the town as a result of the attack by various Serb forces, including, again, the JNA, the unit, Serb police, Serb TO. The attack and take-over included people being driven out of their homes. Non-Serbs were arbitrarily arrested, detained, beaten, sexually assaulted, threatened, included by the accused's unit, and local Serb authorities. And I refer to an adjudicated fact, and I refer to it as AF Roman IV, fact 255, which is noted in the judgement at paragraph 584 in footnote 1207 and in judgement paragraphs 654, 684, 685, and 1081. The Trial Chamber admitted also as an adjudicated fact that: "The clearly recognisable pattern of criminal activity allows for only one reasonable conclusion; namely, that these crimes were committed with the aim of implementing the strategic plan of the Bosnian Serb leadership to take control over the territory claimed for the Serbian state within BiH and to permanently remove the non-Serb population from this territory," AF I, fact 236. The inescapable conclusion from this pattern repeated throughout the indictment area is that the crimes were an integral part of the establishment and maintenance of Serb control, and the accused knew that this pattern of crimes formed an integral part of achieving and maintaining territorial control. The sheer scale and pattern of the crimes in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina makes it inconceivable that the accused would not have known of them. Their functions, by the definition, require Stanisic and Simatovic to be very well informed of issues related to security, and the Trial Chamber's own findings recognises this. The accused knew from April 1991 of the intent of Milan Martic to deport non-Serbs from Krajina. They knew that the SAO Krajina police committed numerous murders and persecution, as well as expelling 80- to 100.000 Croats and other non-Serb civilians. This is at paragraphs 2331 and 2332. The accused also knew their unit committed crimes in Bosanski Samac in April 1992, then sent the same unit to Doboj in early May 1992 where it also committed crimes. This is the judgement, paragraph 2323. And the accused knew of the crimes committed by Arkan and the SDG in the SBWS between September and April -- September 1991 and April 1992 and in Bijeljina and Zvornik from April to September 1992. That is in the judgement, paragraph 2333. And Simatovic and DB operatives were present all over the indictment area, as illustrated in Annex A to the Prosecution's appeal brief. Surely the accused would have been among the best informed about events on the ground at the time. Sorry, I'm having trouble with the technology. Your Honours, the accused were in "direct and frequent contact" with JCE members such as Hadzic, Karadzic, Martic, and Babic, who were the Serb leaders in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina; paragraph 2302. And recall, Your Honours, that the Chamber accepted as an adjudicated fact that the goal of the Bosnian Serbian leadership was to "establish a state in which there would be no place for non-Serbs," AF I, fact 142. In light of their persistence and contacts, the accused would have known of Karadzic's implematic speech in the RS Assembly in 14 October 1991 where he threatened the Bosnian Muslims with extermination if they opted for independence; Exhibit P940. And two months later, Stanisic watched as Karadzic again predicted the death of several hundred thousand people, complete destruction of several hundred towns, and massive population displacements. Stanisic approved Karadzic's statement. And for this, I will have to refer Your Honours to the Prosecution appeal brief at paragraph 26 and Exhibit number 1483. And Stanisic echoed the same intent when he, a few weeks later, told Karadzic that they could "exterminate them completely" in a conversation about Croats; Exhibit P690. There also can be no doubt that the accused knew of the Bosnian Serb leadership's six strategic goals, which included ethnic cleansing. Stanisic attended a meeting in Belgrade on 13 and 14 December 1993 with, among others, Milosevic, Mrksic, Karadzic, Krajisnik, and Mladic, where they discussed the implementation of these six strategic goals; Exhibit P2532 at pages 1 and 2, and judgement paragraph 2310. In conclusion, there can be no doubt that the accused knew that the establishment and maintenance of Serb-dominated regions included the ethnic cleansing of the non-Serb population from those regions. Knowing that the ethnic cleansing of non-Serbs formed an integral part of the establishment of the Serb regions in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, the accused continued to contribute to that goal. For example, though they already, in April 1991, knew of Martic's intent to deport non-Serbs, the accused continued to support Martic and the SAO Krajina police and the Krajina TO over the next year. They played an important role in helping Martic setting up the Krajina police, Simatovic participated in the Lovinac operation in June 1991, knowing the criminal aim of the attack. The accused organised the unit's involvement in the Glina and Struga and operations during which the non-Serb population was expelled. The accused continued to organise training to the SAO Krajina police and TO, and the accused continued arming and supplying the Krajina TO until April 1992. And knowing that the units they had trained in Krajina were committing crimes, the accused continued to train units in the SBWS and along the border of the SBWS in Serbia from September 1991. And knowing of the crimes in Krajina from April 1991, they deployed the unit into operations in the SBWS in September 1991. The accused also financed Arkan and his SDG in 1994 and 1995, including while they were mass murdering non-Serbs in Sanski Most. They also knew of the crimes that Arkan and the SDG had committed in the SBWS in 1991 and in Bijeljina and Zvornik in 1992. They deployed their unit to Bosanski Samac in April 1992 and again to Doboj a few weeks later. In both places, unit members were amongst the notorious abusers of the civilian population. They also deployed the unit to Bratunac and Skelani, which was part of Operation Udar in April 1993, "likely" knowing that Mladic and Mrksic intended ethnic cleansing and knowing of the unit's history of crimes in Bosanski Samac and Doboj. It is thus clear from the Trial Chamber's findings that the accused repeatedly contributed to establishing and maintaining Serb control over large parts of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina knowing that they contributed to ethnic cleansing of those areas. The only reasonable inference from such knowing and protracted contribution is that the accused shared the intent of the common criminal purpose. Your Honours, I should have clarified before I went through all these contributions that while we've been going through this, we have been showing a slide which have the numerous references to the judgement where you find the support for all of these things. I'm sorry I didn't make that clear in the beginning. I hope we may provide Your Honours with copies of the presentation afterwards, and of course we'll give them to the Defence as well, so you will have those references. And so Ms. Jarvis does not have to explain this later, she will later on be using a slide. We'll use the same methodology. Your Honours, so I said, on the facts as found by the Trial Chamber, the accused knowingly and in a protracted way contributed to the implementation of the common criminal purpose. And if Your Honours grant ground 3 of our appeal, other significant contributions are, of course, added; namely, critical support that the accused provided to the establishing and arming of Serb forces in the SBWS, their arming of the Zvornik TO, their deployment of Arkan's SDG in the SBWS, Bijeljina, Zvornik, and Sanski Most where they committed numerous crimes. Your Honours, had the Trial Chamber given consideration to the accused's knowledge of the common criminal purpose, it would have found that the accused shared or had JCE intent. If you do not agree that this is a legal error, then certainly it is a factual error. No reasonable trier of fact could have concluded that the accused did not share the intent of the common criminal purpose given the evidence on record in this case. A clear example of an error of fact is the majority's finding that the accused only knew of a risk of crimes being committed in Krajina by Martic and the SAO Krajina police. We see this error in paragraph 2332. The Trial Chamber found that: "In continuing to support the SAO Krajina police and co-operate with Milan Martic from April 1991, the accused took the risk that the SAO Krajina police would commit crimes when establishing and maintaining Serb control over large areas of Croatia." The majority found that this would be insufficient to meet the intense standard under JCE I. It then concluded that there was another reasonable inference; namely, that the accused intended only to assist the SAO Krajina authorities to establish and maintain territorial control. But the error is that on the Trial Chamber's own findings, the accused knew of Milan Martic's intent to deport and they knew that Milan Martic and the SAO Krajina police were, in fact, expelling and mistreating and killing non-Serbs and participating in operations to expel the non-Serb population. Thus, the accused did not take the risk that crimes would be committed. They knew for certain that the crimes would be committed. The majority's conclusion that there was only a risk of crimes was patently unreasonable. Considering the accused's repeated and extensive support to Milan Martic and the SAO Krajina police, the only conclusion available was that the accused intended the crimes. Your Honours, to sum up, the Trial Chamber's do inferences on the accused's intent without considering the relevant question: Whether the accused knew of the common purpose, knew that crimes were an integral part of achievement of territorial control in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is at the heart of this case. Not addressing this question led to its failure to consider evidence clearly relevant to the existence of the common criminal purpose and thus, in turn, to intent. By failing to make findings on those facts which are essential to the determination of the guilt and by making an insufficient analysis of evidence, the Trial Chamber failed to provide a reasoned opinion. The Trial Chamber thereby erred in law. As I've mentioned, Your Honours, if you do not agree that this is an error of law, the Prosecution has certainly demonstrated that the Trial Chamber committed an error of fact. Either way, the intent analysis in this case is so obviously erroneous that it must be corrected. Ms. Jarvis will now address Your Honours on how to apply an appropriate remedy.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, as we've demonstrated throughout our argument so far, the judgement contains numerous fatal errors that must be corrected. This then raises the question what should be done. If the outcome of correcting the legal or factual errors that we have argued is that the acquittals are invalidated, the Appeals Chamber has the power to substitute convictions in their place. This power has been repeatedly confirmed and exercised by the Appeals Chamber, most recently in the Popovic et al. case, concerning crimes committed by Mr. Pandurevic. We acknowledge that in the present case, the Appeals Chamber would be substituting convictions for outright acquittals. However, the principle involved is no different from when substituting convictions for partial acquittals, as the Appeals Chamber has done on many occasions before. The Appeals Chamber has found it does not violate the accused's rights to enter convictions on appeal with no further right to appeal. The accused raises no new arguments in this regard. So there is no doubt that the Appeals Chamber has the authority to correct the errors in this case and to make the necessary findings to enter convictions. We say there are two main reasons why Your Honours should exercise that power here. First, as I've mentioned, the Appeals Chamber has been willing to engage in fact-finding to correct errors in other cases. In particular, in Bizumungu, the ICTR Appeals Chamber found a failure to provide a reasoned opinion because the Trial Chamber had failed to enter any legal findings on some parts of the crime base. As a result, it had failed to address "the most fundamental of issues." That's Bizimungu appeal judgement at paragraph 19. Notwithstanding the fundamental nature of the errors, the Appeals Chamber proceeded to review the record and to determine whether the Trial Chamber's convictions could be sustained on appeal. Second, we should not necessarily assume that the extent of the fact-finding or the nature of the fact-finding required in this case would be unacceptably extensive or complicated. In Bizimungu, the Appeals Chamber was able to make the missing mens rea findings, including on crimes like genocide, primarily by situating the underlying criminal acts in the context of the systemic destructive campaign going on across Rwanda at the time, assessed in light of the accused's knowledge of that prevailing context. Essentially the same process is required here. This is a case about looking at the acts and statements of the accused in the proper context of the prevailing campaign of ethnic cleansing across the three regions in the indictment. Your Honours, look at the patterns of crimes across the three regions. Look at what the accused knew. Look at who they worked together closely with over a period of four years. Look at what they did and did not do. The watching world clearly understood what was going on in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina during the indictment period to the point where the very term "ethnic cleansing" became part of our contemporary vocabulary. The victims in the villages systematically attacked, cleansed, and razed, they certainly understood what was going on. It's inconceivable that the two accused in this case did not also clearly understand what was going on. Further, as Mr. Marcussen and I have explained throughout our submissions today, the problems in the majority's analysis of shared intent stem from two key omissions: First, the majority's failure to make findings on the existence of the common criminal purpose to ethnically cleanse; and, second, the majority's failure to consider the repeated contributions of the accused in light of their knowledge of that common criminal purpose. Correcting these two omissions need not necessarily be heavily fact-intensive. Although the Trial Chamber failed to consider these two crucial factors in its intent analysis, the Trial Chamber made extensive underlying findings elsewhere in the judgement that are highly relevant to these issues, if only it had addressed them in its analysis of intent. To give you an idea of what I mean -- and we have a slide which contains the references for the propositions that I will explain. The Trial Chamber accepted that there was a massive expulsion campaign in Krajina between April 1991 and April 1992. It accepted that Martic, the Croatian Serb political leader in Krajina, had the intent to deport non-Serbs and used tools under his control, the Krajina police and TO, to commit the crimes in furtherance of this purpose. It accepted that Stanisic and Simatovic supported and assisted these tools consistently over a year with knowledge of Martic's intent and of the crimes committed. The Chamber expressly accepted that attacks on specific towns in SAO Krajina and SAO SBWS were "aimed at forcing the local population to leave in order to establish a purely Serb territory." The Trial Chamber further found that there was a single widespread and discriminatory attack across the three regions directed against the non-Serb civilian population. The accused and their unit then continued to contribute towards the operations to take territorial control in SAO SBWS and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your Honours, given the accused's knowledge that the crimes were integral to the process of taking and maintaining territorial control and their knowledge that massive crimes were in fact being committed in furtherance of that common criminal purpose, the only reasonable inference to draw from their continued assistance again and again over a period of years is that they shared the intent. Similarly, the amount of fact-finding required to provide a remedy for the Prosecution's alternative ground concerning aiding and abetting need not be extensive, particularly with the erroneous specific direction standard removed from the equation, the Trial Chamber's existing findings provide an important foundation for entering aiding and abetting convictions. We accept, of course, Your Honours, the importance of providing a process that is fair to the accused. In Bizimungu, the ICTR Appeals Chamber, following the oral argument, ordered additional written briefings by the parties in order to provide them with a full and focused opportunity to address the sufficiency of the Trial Chamber's findings and the evidence on the record to support the convictions erroneously entered by the Trial Chamber. That's Bizimungu appeal judgement at paragraph 24. Your Honours could, of course, consider extending a similar opportunity to the parties here. Ultimately though, Your Honours, the appropriate remedy lies within your discretion. Should you determine that this is not an appropriate case for the Appeals Chamber to correct the errors, you should remit the matter to another Chamber. This wouldn't be a retrial but a process of remitting for re-adjudication based on the evidence already adduced at trial. Again, it would be for Your Honours to determine the remit parameters, but it would be important to ensure that instructions to the remand Bench contain precise information about the nature of the Trial Chamber's errors and the correct procedure for them to follow. In particular, these instructions should include directions to consider, among other things: The missing pieces of the Trial Chamber's JCE analysis - namely, whether the alleged common criminal purpose existed, and, if so, its nature and scope; the key JCE members; the tools used by the JCE to commit the crimes; and, most importantly, what the accused knew about the common criminal purpose, the crimes involved, the tools used, and the crimes committed in furtherance of it. Should Your Honours decline to order any of the remedies so far suggested, then you should order a retrial. However, in our submission, a retrial is not the most appropriate remedy in this case. Here the problem is not with the existing evidentiary record. The problem is one of failure to properly adjudicated the evidence already on that record. The interests of justice militate away from a time and resource-intensive retrial and towards a remedy that will correct the problem at issue. In conclusion, the fatal errors in the majority's analysis must be corrected. Doing nothing is not an option in a case where there has been a fundamental failure to adjudicate the relevant issues before the Chamber, leaving the promise of justice for the victim community, and indeed the international community, completely unfulfilled. This is a JCE case, and to accurately reflect the culpability of the accused, they should be convicted under the JCE framework.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: The outcome of this appeal has implications for international criminal law but most of all for the victims. The Appeals Chamber's intervention is crucial to safe-guard the legacy of this Tribunal and the interests of justice in this case. The Appeals Chamber must find a way to ensure that justice is finally done. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
