utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Any other questions by my colleagues? If that's not the case, then we can now break and we will reconvene at 1.00 for the -- first the response of counsel for Mr. Stanisic and later for Mr. Simatovic. So we break now for one hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So we resume the hearing, and I will invite counsel for Mr. Stanisic to respond for one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon. On the 30th of May 2013, more than ten years after his arrest, Mr. Stanisic was acquitted of all charges against him. Whilst he always denied involvement in the crimes, he understood and continues to understand that occupying a senior role in the Serbian government at that time in the face of such terrible crimes meant that questions had to be asked and answered, justice had to be done, and it had to be seen to be done. However, justice is often a slow and cumbersome process, and it comes with significant costs. It is especially slow and costly when Prosecutors overload indictments with allegations that advance flamboyant claims that one individual is in command of every single political and military structure and therefore responsible for every crime across thousands of square kilometres, along with associated undiscerning claims that every member of the Serb forces is a criminal acting in furtherance of a campaign of violence against civilians. For over ten years, Mr. Stanisic has faced these allegations and the threat of a life sentence, and these proceedings have cost him dearly, including undermining his right to liberty, his family life, and his health. He spent nearly five years in prison on these charges during which time his mental health and physical health deteriorated. He was found unfit to stand trial for more than one year. The trial had to be modified to compensate for his ill health, limited to only two to three days per week and breaks every 75 minutes. Some might say, well, that's the price of accountability. And, let's face it, he was in a senior position, the Trial Chamber did make some findings that suggest he might have been involved in crime. So perhaps he was lucky. Why should he complain? However, the Trial Chamber considered allegations that spanned across Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina for more than five years, and the majority found, time and time and time again that there was reasonable doubt as to his guilt. If that is to mean anything, then it must mean that we recognise that Mr. Stanisic has paid a considerable price as a result of proceedings that led to his acquittal. It's the administration of justice as well as these costs that ought to way heavily upon any prosecutor when deciding the parameters of an appeal. The appellate jurisdiction is a narrow one, and intentionally so. It's not designed to provide a disgruntled party with another bite at the cherry. It's not an opportunity to relitigate or regurgitate trial arguments in the hope that another set of Judges will come to a different conclusion. As we have argued in our response and continue to argue in the next hour, this appellant has taken another approach. Instead of a cautious appeal that accords with appellate review standards, the appellant's arguments circumvent basic axioms of appellate litigation, pay insufficient heed to due process considerations, and ultimately fail to enhance the administration of justice. Even if the appellant's arguments had merit and even if they had not taken this unfortunate approach, this appeal is doubtful and controversial. Consider in the first place that a person convicted of a criminal offence is entitled, as is his fundamental human right, to a review of that conviction, and indeed any sentence imposed, in a higher tribunal established by law. That principle is enshrined, inter alia, in Article 14(5) of the ICCPR. Yet the Prosecution invites the Court to enter a conviction in this appeal for the first time, despite the unavailability of any review by a higher tribunal. The respondent's conviction in this court which the appellant urges upon you will be both the first and also the final pronouncement of their guilt.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could you please slow down? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Given that it would follow that the Prosecution getting two bites at the cherry, the irony in that is supreme. We submit that the Appeals Chamber is bound to apply the power accorded it under Article 25(2) in a manner that complies with fundamental human rights, including the right to have any conviction reviewed by a superior tribunal. As the UN Human rights Committee has said explicitly in its general comment on the subject, and I am quoting here: "Article 14, paragraph 5, is violated not only if the decision by the court of first instance is final but also where a conviction imposed by an appeal court or a court of final instance following acquittal by a lower court, according to domestic law cannot be reviewed by a higher court," that's general comment 32; Terron versus Spain. Nothing in Article 25 of this Statute even remotely suggests that this fundamental right has been abrogated, even assuming for a moment that the Security Council could have been competent to abrogate such a fundamental protection. Indeed, quite the contrary. Article 25 makes clear that the Prosecutor on appeal must demonstrate you one of two things in order to obtain appellate relief. Under Article 25(1)(a), the Prosecutor must show that the Trial Chamber not only has erred in law but has done so in a way which invalidates the judgement. And even higher threshold exists under 25(1)(b). There it must be shown by the Prosecutor that there has been an error of fact by the Trial Chamber and that it is of such a serious and total magnitude as to have occasioned a miscarriage of justice. A very, very high threshold indeed. And yet as with every point in this case, the Prosecution takes the position, which we say is impossibly ambitious, that the appellate relief it should have in this case is the substitution of an acquittal for a conviction without the prospect of any review and the imposition of a life sentence again beyond review. No explanation is given as to how Article 25(2) read together with Article 25(1) and in the context of the Statute as a whole could be permitted to produce a result which the Human Rights Committee has stated is unlawful. 168 states around the world are obliged to adhere to this minimum standard. The appellant fails to proffer any reason why the ICTY should be any different and why it should be set on a collision course with the Human Rights Committee of the same United Nations. The argument is one of jurisdiction, not discretion. If Article 25 is capable of being read in a way that preserves a fundamental right, and it plainly can be here, then it should be. Now, the Appeals Chamber may well feel in this case that the substantive grounds of appeal can simply be dismissed out of hand. There is no merit in them. But we do not shy away from this fundamental point: If the Chamber finds some apparent prima facie merit lurking through the Prosecution's scatter-gun appeal grounds, the Chamber could not, concomitant with its position as a judicial institution, go on to impose conviction and sentence. Especially not without detailed submissions from the Prosecution explaining why it has the jurisdiction to do that. Moreover, the respondents have been provided with an hour only to address the Chamber. If there is anything attractive in the Prosecution's regurgitation, we submit on behalf of Mr. Stanisic, that we have insufficient time and notice to be able to confront the real points of this appeal - the real points that might now be in the Chamber's mind as potentially leading to conviction and sentence. Moreover, what a curious position the respondent finds himself in, defending an attempt to send him to prison for life with the Prosecution having the last word later on today. Putting these jurisdictional issues aside, I will now move to a discussion about the correct approach to appellate standards in the context of this appeal. This will be followed by a discussion as to how the appellant seeks to circumvent them. The proper approach. In large part, this appeal, according to the appellant's arguments in ground 1 and ground 2, involve alleged errors of law. We will not address you further on ground 3 and the alleged errors of fact unless you wish. It is so utterly devoid of merit we will not dedicate any time to these issues. However, ground 1 and ground 2 risk obscuring the real issues, and we hope to be able to assist the Appeals Chamber in uncovering the strategy that lies beneath. As the appellant is undoubtedly aware, when the Appeals Chamber finds an error of law, it applies it to the factual findings. Only if there are no relevant factual findings does the Appeals Chamber look at the evidence in the trial record. In other words, it's not sufficient for the appellant to demonstrate an error of law. It must demonstrate to you that any relevant factual findings that it then wishes to avoid are conclusions that no reasonable trier of fact could have made and that such findings occasioned a miscarriage of justice. This is critical in this appeal. In subground (1)(A), the appellant urges that the majority's -- argues that the majority's manifest legal error in failing to adjudicate or provide a reasoned opinion on the objective existence of a common criminal purpose and the contribution of the accused to that criminal purpose led to an error that invalidates the judgement. It also contends that the Trial Chamber's failure to address the common criminal purpose properly is illustrated by its assessment of the accused's actions as contributions to certain crimes but not as contributions to the common criminal purpose. As must be plain to the Appeals Chamber and to the appellant, even if there is merit to this argument, this legal error could not conceivably render every factual finding favourable to the accused in error. At best, it could only have impacted upon specific findings, such as the final assessments concerning shared intent, but it could not conceivably render underlying factual findings that address the conduct of JCE members or their tools or those acting lawfully, including Mr. Stanisic, and their interaction in error. For example, the appellant accepts at paragraph 23 of the appeal that the Trial Chamber did make findings concerning the accused's contributions to certain crimes. The appellant doesn't want to the admit that the Chamber, in making these assessments, was talking about the criminal means of the JCE alleged and not only specific criminal events. But putting that aside, they accept these findings were made. This is a critical admission. It means that the Trial Chamber had the raw building blocks for a reasoned assessment of JCE liability that may not now be brushed aside by the appellant in their relitigation attempt. It means, in short, that even if the Trial Chamber erred in failing to adjudicate or provide sufficient reasoning on the common criminal purpose, there are scores and scores of findings that remain untouched. As the Appeals Chamber has made clear in Krajisnik, it's the common objective that begins to transform a plurality of persons into a group or enterprise, as this plurality has in common the particular objective. The persons in a criminal enterprise must be shown to act together in concert with each other in the implementation of a common objective if they are to share responsibility for the crimes committed through the JCE. As Your Honours will appreciate, the assessment of the significance of an accused's contribution is critical. First, the significant contribution an accused makes to the various crimes within the common purpose amounts to the individual actus reus. An accurate measurement of contribution is indispensable. Second, a trier of fact may rely upon it to establish by inference that the accused possessed the requisite mens rea for the crimes adjudged. Of course, this argument is not to be confused with the claim that the accused must have made a criminal contribution to the common purpose. We accept an individual may contribute to a criminal purpose through noncriminal behaviour. However, that contribution must be to further the criminal means. In this case, the Trial Chamber followed precisely these requirements. It assessed Stanisic's contribution to each of the criminal means and not, as the appellant suggests, only specific crimes, and used those findings of fact to infer that he harboured no shared criminal intent to further the common criminal purpose. In short, and this is what the appellant seeks to get around, and must get around: Having found that a reasonable inference existed that he was over the five-year indictment period, consistently acting in furtherance of lawful military objectives, not the criminal means, the majority was duty-bound to acquit him. In these circumstances, we need to look at the judgement. The factual findings that the appellant accepts were made concerning the respondent's contributions to crimes must still stand, as must many of the related findings that address such things that the contributions of state security men, who the appellant alleges were tools of the joint criminal enterprise, the contributions of perpetrators to crimes, the occurrence and pattern of crimes, the interactions of many of the protagonists, including the perpetrators, the interactions - and I emphasize this - the interactions of those involved in lawful activity, and so on and so forth. If the appellant wishes to take issue with these facts, then they may, but only through on demonstration of a lack of reasonableness and a resulting miscarriage of justice. If the appellant is able to identify errors of fact in these calculations, then they must argue them. Not disregard them. Of course, as the appellant appreciates, given the systemic and wholly reasonable way the majority reasoned their way through these predicate JCE findings and the paucity of factual findings suggesting that Stanisic was in any way interacting with alleged perpetrators in pursuance of the criminal means, their argument never gets off the ground. Similarly in ground 1(B), the appellant seeks to argue that the Trial Chamber erred by misapplying the burden of proof. They allege the evidence was considered piecemeal and that the reasonable doubt standard was applied to individual pieces of evidence. Let's assume that's correct for a moment. That still leaves all factual findings in place; that is, sections 3, 4, and 6 of the Trial Chamber judgement, that outlines in details the crimes of murder, persecution, deportation, and forcible transfer. The perpetrators who they were, their interaction in furtherance of crime, their individual interaction in furtherance of military activity, not crimes, and Stanisic's role and interaction with those events and the findings that he was interacting in furtherance of lawful activity. If ground (B) has merit, then all that is left for the Appeals Chamber to do, we submit, is remit the case to the Trial Chamber for them to consider all these factual findings in light of the correct legal standard and apply the standard and burden of proof to the factual findings already made. Similarly, with regard to ground 2, the appellant asserts an alleged error of law in relation to the requirement of specific direction. On the face of it, there is nothing to suppose that error, if indeed it was, impacts upon the factual findings made. The findings relating to remoteness, proximity and so on remain untouched, unless the appellant demonstrates otherwise. Having appreciated the detailed nature of the judgement and these legal cul de sacs, the appellant then changes course. The appellant attempts to sidestep these facts and relitigate the points. How do they do that? Well, they engage in a legal and factual four-step process, a forensic dance that aims to relitigate hundreds of factual findings without the required demonstration of error.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think there should be a slide at this point, slide 1, which shows in summary the approach the appellant takes to this appeal. We're going to deal with two or three examples of this four-step shuffle, but it's an approach that taints the whole appeal and each and every argument on scores and scores of facts and factual findings made that the appellant seeks to circumvent and get around. Step 1, the appellant takes a selection of factual findings they like, those that serve the purpose of beginning the litigation afresh. As we shall see shortly, their immediate focus is to establish the presence of Stanisic or his associates in the war zones. Step 2, the appellant disregards certain inconvenient factual findings without attempting to demonstrate that the Trial Chamber erred in fact or law. This enables its favourite facts from step 1 to be stripped of context ready to be reassembled in step 3. Step 3, in place of the inconvenient factual findings, the appellant uses the step 1 findings, reassembles them to produce the factual findings that it wishes the Trial Chamber had made, and it does this through calling upon tangential findings from the judgement and apparently incriminatory evidence from the trial record. Of course, there is no attempt at balance or explanation. The material is chosen because it might make the respondent look guilty and cast doubt upon the reasoned decisions by the majority. At the very least, whether we're right about this or not, the appellant has a lot to explain to be able to parachute 260 pieces of evidence from the trial record into this appeal, not counting the reintroduction of a plethora of adjudicated facts as this appellant seeks to do. The requirement to prioritise findings over evidence is, of course, in accord with the notion of a Trial Chamber's core function as a finder of fact. Of course, the Appeals Chamber is aware of this and will not likely disturb findings of fact by the Trial Chamber. Such an approach also avoids having the Appeals Chamber engage excessively in fact-finding and the weighing of evidence that, as noted in the Gotovina case, substantially comprises fair trial rights. And, finally, the appellant in step 4 tops off this relitigation with a nice presumption of guilt. Having reconstructed the factual findings and evidence, the final step in the appellant's methodology is to encourage the Appeals Chamber to attribute guilt by association using an all-encompassing presumption of guilt. That starts from an absurdity that was advanced at trial, roundly rejected by the majority that every action by any member of the Serbian political and military organisations must have been in furtherance of crime and every action was part of the campaign of violence against civilians. We heard it this morning on a number of occasions when we heard from the appellant that we should start from the proposition that these operations to take territorial control were about ethnic cleansing. We heard it from the appellant this morning when they said the Chamber had to assume that crimes were an inherent part of the take-over operation. That's the only way the appellant gets home, a presumption of guilt. Findings that crimes were an inherent component of the whole operations, findings not made by the Trial Chamber; in fact, the contrary found by the Trial Chamber throughout the judgement. The bank robbery example is entirely inapposite but it does demonstrate one thing: The Prosecution's presumption of guilt. Their driver drives a car to the bank to rob it, while actually in this case the majority found that the driver drove the men to the bank to withdraw money lawfully and that others robbed the bank subsequently. There is a distinction here. The distinction reflected in the factual findings and a distinction which doesn't rely upon a presumption of guilt that the only thing going on was the robbing of a bank. This allegation was rightly rejected by the majority after detailed evidence was submitted, after Stanisic Defence ran a whole defence on the basis that Stanisic was participating in lawful war activity, they heard the evidence and concluded the Prosecution's presumption of only one thing going on was wrong. Let's now turn to some specifics about their de novo review. This de novo review places this Chamber or attempts to place this Chamber in the invidious position of having to rule on core issues of culpability if, indeed, their approach is accepted, without the benefit of a balanced view of 4.843 exhibits and effectively several years of trial testimony. That the majority found consistently was at odds with this prevailing notion that the only thing going on was a campaign of violence against civilians. The judgement is full of it. Defensive operations, operations to seize territory without crimes and crimes. An examination of the appellant's four-step strategy is instructive. It has nothing to do with errors of law being corrected and this correct standard being applied to the findings made. At paragraphs 51 and 52 of the appeal, and we'll just throw that up onto the screen, slide 2, we can see what this de novo review is designed to achieve. They want to reargue their case. But given the accused's authority over the SDB, the State Security Service, no reasonable Chamber could conclude that the consistent deployment of SDB assets to implement the common criminal purpose occurred without the accused's knowledge and volition. Of course, as I have just noted, that's not what the majority found. They didn't find consistent deployment to implement a common criminal purpose. They found a consistent deployment in pursuit of lawful activity. But putting that aside for a moment. Step 1, looking at Golubic. Golubic was the first training camp which the Prosecution suggested was effectively the beginning or part of the beginning of the joint criminal enterprise. What does the Prosecution's four-step shuffle involve? In paragraphs 51 and 52 of their appeal, the Appeals Chamber is urged to begin looking at Annex A of the Prosecution's appeal, which contains findings, we are told, that the appellant has been shown to have DB assets throughout the war zones. Doesn't "assets" have a nice sinister ring to it? Sounds much better than DB employees or associates. Sounds even better than DB employers or -- employees or associates found consistently to have been acting lawfully. However, these are the findings the appellant likes because they represent a chance to begin again, as if a three-year fiercely contested trial never took place. These are the foundations of the new house the appellant wants to build. For example, Annex A contains factual findings, as I've said, relating to Golubic. Annex A lists a number of paragraphs of the judgement that address the Chamber's findings that State Security employees or associates created, financed, and managed Golubic. Of course, the findings that the appellant relies upon - paragraphs 1366 and 1367 and 1421 of the judgement - shows only the bear facts of the accused's interactions with perpetrators of crimes, such as Martic and Captain Dragan, as well as the establishment of the unit. According to the appellant's case at trial, the training camp was created in furtherance of the criminal purpose. This case was rejected at trial. However, as we shall see, the appellant makes no attempt to address these findings. On the contrary, as we move to step 2 of the appellant's relitigation strategy, Annex A merely reiterates the factual findings that establish the presence of DB assets and nothing more. Step 2, disregarding the Trial Chamber's factual findings. Of course, the collective pursuit of a common purpose with identical criminal intent is what defines membership in a JCE plurality --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speaker is kindly requested to speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. Having established that DB operatives were physically present in and around Golubic, the appellant seeks to disregard the Trial Chamber's findings that provide cogent evidence relevant to the question of action in furtherance of criminal purposes. They fail to bring to the Appeals Chamber's attention a series of findings in paragraph 2197 of the judgement that shows the training at Golubic was of a military nature and included weapons and ambush training, as well as the treatment of prisoners of war and the treatment of civilians in armed conflict. Of course these findings weighed heavily on the majority's deliberations, weighed heavily on the finding that this camp, Stanisic's interactions, did not allow it to infer he was acting in furtherance of common criminal purpose. Obviously if a training camp is set up and the recruits are being trained to obey the laws of war, this is a finding which is extremely relevant. Not according to the appellant's relitigation strategy. Step 3 then reassembles these narrowed findings. They begin to reconstruct so that these factual findings and cherry-picked evidence from the trial record looks like Stanisic's participation might have been a contribution to a criminal purpose. At paragraph 61 of the appeal, the appellant suggests that Stanisic and Martic had agreed on the creation of a training camp at Martic's headquarters in the Golubic and that the accused also brokered the deployment of "JCE sympathiser Captain Dragan." At paragraph 62, the apparently reiterates the establishment of the unit at Golubic and its alleged "support to the parallel security structures and other Serb forces that were allegedly part of the criminal purpose." We are then reminded that the unit members trained at Golubic went on to establish and train further units that participated in attacks against non-Serbs in Krajina, suggesting that Stanisic was responsible for these crimes, and so it goes on. So the appellant wants to build a new house only using the structures they fancy and disregarding the rest, without showing why some of those structures without -- why the windows, why the doors and so on, cannot be used again, because they are not convenient for the Prosecution. And so we move to the appellant's step 4, coupe de grace. Having reconstructed the factual findings and evidence from the trial record so the appellant now appears to have been acting in furtherance of the criminal purpose, the appellant then parachutes into the mix their presumption of guilt. As we laid out with particularity and in our response and in our closing brief at trial, not a single Prosecution or Defence witness provided evidence that allowed a reasonable trier of fact to conclude that Golubic was created in furtherance of a common criminal purpose. And it's worth repeating: Not a single Prosecution witness gave evidence to that effect. And here we have relitigation, ignoring their own witnesses at trial. And then at section III of the appeal, we leap from Golubic, as the Trial Chamber found it, to JCE members, including the accused, created and used armed groups in Croatia to further the common criminal purpose, to parallel structures controlling the events to Serb forces in 3(b) of their appeal unleashing and escalating a systemic campaign of ethnic cleansing across Croatia. And so the circle is squared. I respectfully invite the Chamber to also look at slide 4 as another illustration of this step 4 process in relation this time to Operation Udar in Skelani. I'm not going to take time to go through it, but it's exactly the same, and if we had the time, we could go through almost every single assertion made by the appellant and show this four-step process. Why did they take this approach? Why so much struggling with the factual findings? Because the majority got it right. It is a careful and nuanced judgement that, unlike the appellant's over-generalised indictment and case at trial, ascends to make legal and factual distinctions, the legal and factual distinctions that were required. They may not like them but they're made, and they're nuanced, and they're careful, and they're detailed. Section 3 to 4 of the judgement goes well beyond what was required in setting out the crimes and the criminal means, the perpetrators and the nature of their interaction in furtherance of war and crime and lawful activity. This enabled the Chamber to view whether there existed a common criminal plan that amounted to or involved the commission of the crimes alleged and to view with utmost clarity whether a plurality of persons acted in concert and pursuit of a common criminal purpose. Section 6 of the judgement takes the same painstaking approach to the third objective aspect of the alleged JCE, the participation by the accused in the form of a contribution to the common criminal plan or otherwise in pursuit of lawful activity. These factual findings allowed the Chamber to assess whether the intention of the accused was identical to those pursuing crime and whether any shared intent to commit crime encompassed the entire scope of the common purpose alleged. In light of these carefully laid-out details in the sections I've just mentioned, the appellant's proposition that the majority did not have the precise material necessary to make the careful assessments about the accused's intent is utterly devoid of merit, and their attempt to avoid the factual findings is a manifest demonstration of that fact. The majority's factual findings summed up in paragraph 2335 of the judgement reflected those detailed assessments of the crimes, the interactions in pursuit of the crimes, the pattern of the crimes, and so on. Paragraph 2335 sums up: "Stanisic's lack of participation in the criminal means; two, his consistent contribution to military activity against Croat forces, not civilians; Bosnian forces or Bosnian Muslim forces, not civilians; and the consistent activity over the five-year indictment period of acting in furtherance of seizing control over territory, not forcibly displacing or deporting civilians." We submit not only was there ample reasonable doubt as to shared intent, but no reasonable trier of fact could have found differently. Having made these detailed findings which, of course, start with contribution to criminal means, the Chamber did not have to go back to its factual assessments that are described in minute details and write up the criminal purpose that the appellant wants, we suspect, for the historical record, not because it's required in this case. As slide 5 of our submissions show, the correct position about what the majority did is as follows. The OTP alleged that Stanisic's shared intent should be approached in the following way. You'll see this from their closing brief. They said to the Trial Chamber: You can infer Stanisic's shared intent from (a) his massive and complex arming and training screams and their repeated deployment to special units; and (b) in addition to these overarching schemes, three discrete examples of actions or words that irrefutably demonstrate he shared the intent. As our slide 6 shows, taken from the trial judgement 2306 and 2317 and sections 3 to 4 and 6.9 of the judgement, rather than taking a piecemeal approach to the evidence, the Trial Chamber did precisely what was urged upon them by the Prosecution at trial. To now allege errors of law and fact when they urged that approach on the Trial Chamber is more than a little curious. To do so following a four-step strategy that sidesteps the Trial Chamber's factual findings should only lead to one result: The summary dismissal of ground 1 of the appeal or dismissal on its merits. Moving to ground 2. Under ground 2, the aiding and abetting ground, we would like to take -- we would like to start by taking a step back and assuming for a moment that the Sainovic and Popovic findings that specific direction is not an essential element of the actus reus of aiding and abetting is the prevailing law. The question, of course, is how, if at all, does the Trial Chamber's error of law impact upon Stanisic's acquittals. As an examination of the precise legal and factual findings in this case show, not much actually turns on this error of law. It certainly does not invalidate the acquittals, and it certainly does not permit the appellant to engage once more with the four-step process of reconstruction and relitigation. This is evidence in the plain words of the judgement. The appellant accepts that the Trial Chamber took the following approach which is summed up in paragraph 1264 of the trial judgement: (1) it outlined the law as it understood it from Perisic, and then it took the following step. The Trial Chamber sought specific direction as a step towards assessing whether the respondent's acts had substantially contributed to the crimes; and, (2), it drew the following conclusions in express terms in section 6 entitled "The accused's responsibility," namely, that on the facts such substantial effect had not been established. To even get home or even get in the door of this ground of appeal, the Prosecution must show that the Trial Chamber could, in view of its factual findings, have reasonably come to only one conclusion; namely, that the accused's acts, done knowingly, had a substantial effect on the crimes. On any fair reading of the trial judgement, we submit, that is an insurmountable burden for the appellant to discharge. Paragraphs 2359 to 2361 of the trial judgement makes clear that the analysis conducted under the rubric of specific direction was precisely that required for a proper understanding of substantial effect and the mens rea of aiding and abetting. For example, at paragraph 2360, the Chamber lays out the factors it considered in reaching the conclusion that Stanisic's acts were not specifically directed to crimes. The Chamber's analysis encompassed all factors that could have been examined as specific direction, but without a shadow of doubt, according to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, had to be considered by any reasonable Trial Chamber in deciding substantial effect, whether or not it was correct to require that specific direction be considered as an analytically distinct element. The appellant continues to neglect this critical factor in its appeal. Specifically in relation to the crimes in Bosanski Samac, Doboj, and the SAO Krajina, these included issues that went to establishing the accused's links to the crimes, including wide-ranging issue that went to proximity and remoteness and propinquity. The type and scale of the assistance, the fact that the accused acted consistently lawfully, command and control of the unit, the training of the unit in laws of war, the lack of presence at the scene of the crimes during their commission, the giving of lawful commands to the unit, and so on and so forth. Having taken that holistic analytical approach unimpeachably, we say, the Trial Chamber reached two findings in paragraph 2361 which are fatal to much of the appellant's ground 2 appeal: "The majority recalls its findings on the accused's mens rea, see chapters 6.9 and 6.10, i.e., that they lacked mens rea, and," and this is the crucial point the Prosecution cannot overcome: "Its finding that the kind of assistance rendered to the unit, the group most closely linked to the accused, is insufficient to incur criminal responsibility as an aider and abetter." We emphasize on the phrase "the kind of assistance." The Trial Chamber was not here saying anything about specific direction. It found in the clearest possible terms that the acts done by the accused were simply too insubstantial, too remote in time, space, and causative effect to have had the required effect on the perpetration of the crimes; that is to say, not only were the acts not specifically directed at the offending, they were not, but the connection between those acts and the criminality was far from sufficiently strong to amount to a substantial effect on that criminality. The majority's analysis is eminently reasonable. It certainly falls well within the discretion accorded to any Trial Chamber. Unfortunately, the appellant, instead of confronting the relevant factual findings, attempts once again to sidestep the issues through their four-step forensic shuffle. Given that time is short, I will focus on the appellant's submissions concerning Bosanski Samac and Doboj. Step one, taking the findings they like. In ground 2(B), at paragraph 158, the appellant lists the factors that they say ought to have been decisive in establishing substantial effect in Bosanski Samac and Doboj. According to the appellant, having lawfully trained the unit, loaned it to others, and financed it during the commission of the crimes, no reasonable trier of fact could have found that these contributions did not have a substantial effect on the commission of the crimes. No need to look at anything else, according to the appellant. And as note in our response, at paragraphs 124 to 128, the prevailing jurisprudence of this Tribunal, all of it decided before Perisic, from the appellant's favourite case, Furundzija, to Aleksovski, to Blagojevic, to Simic, and so on, all of it suggests that in order to properly assess the actus reus and mens rea of aiding and abetting, various factors that go to proximity and remoteness must be taken into account. Obviously the jurisprudence does not permit the appellant to ignore every single factor but the bear fact that the respondent created and loaned and financed a unit, clearly. But that's where we are with their step 1 relitigation. Step 2. What were the factors ignored? The lack of command and control over the unit during the commission of crimes, see paragraph 2335 of the judgement; the training on the laws of war of the unit at paragraph 1369, 2917, 2329; lack of knowledge of the crimes, paragraphs 2323 of the judgement; lack of presence at the scene of the crimes, paragraphs 2360. And what we pointed out in the response that the appellant was ignoring all of these relevant findings, we have a curious reply: "The Chamber's findings demonstrate that Stanisic and Simic provided the unit with structure, preparedness, resources, and equipment to participate in the take-overs of Bosanski Samac and Doboj; therefore, aiding and abetting is established." Really? Established from those bear facts, ignoring everything else? To compound this unfortunate approach, the appellant then claims at paragraph 163 of the appeal that the majority made no mens rea findings. In doing so, they close their eyes once more to that which is inconvenient. As set out in paragraph 2323, the Trial Chamber found that: "Given their role vis-à-vis the unit set out above and the scope of the crimes, the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the accused must have known that the unit members committed crimes in Bosanski Samac. Subsequently, in the awareness that the unit members had committed crimes in Bosanski Samac, the accused organised the unit's involvement in the Doboj operations. Although the unit's composition differed between the Bosanski Samac and Doboj operations, the Trial Chamber considers that, after the Bosanski Samac crimes it may have been reasonably foreseeable to the accused that unit members would commit crimes in Doboj." In other words, the majority found that Stanisic did not know of the crimes in Bosanski Samac until after their commission and that they were not even reasonably foreseeable to him. As for Doboj, it may have been reasonably foreseeable in Doboj that the unit might commit crimes. In other words, Stanisic did not know that his actions in loaning the unit would assist the commission of crimes, nor was he aware he of the essential element of those crimes, including the intent of the unit members. Applying the burden and the standard of proof, the majority could not be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt. And, of course, when you actually look at these findings in context, these findings are more than reasonable. Over five years, the findings make clear that the unit acted lawfully except in two operations: Bosanski Samac and Doboj. After the commission of crimes by a handful of men from the unit in Bosanski Samac, different members of the unit were sent to Doboj; i.e., those that had not committed crimes in Bosanski Samac. We would say the majority was actually too generous towards the Prosecution case. If different men from the unit were sent to Doboj, why was it reasonably foreseeable or why may it have been reasonably foreseeable to Mr. Stanisic that those different men, who had no criminal past, would commit crimes in Bosanski Samac? The Chamber failed to see a reasonable inference arose, that the men who committed crimes in Doboj -- sorry, in Bosanski Samac, were not sent to Doboj because they had been taken out of action because of crimes in Bosanski Samac. We shall never know, the Prosecution failed to explore that point at trial, but it's a reasonable inference. Which brings me to the third strategy, the third step in their resembling relitigation process. In relation to Bosanski Samac and the finding in paragraph 2326, that Stanisic only knew of the unit's crimes afterwards, the appellant attempts to reconstruct a new mens rea finding. In paragraphs 16 and 65 of the appeal, the appellant contends that Stanisic knew the unit would commit crimes in Bosanski Samac, not because the unit had acted criminally before, not because it showed any propensity to commit crimes, not because it had received orders to commit crimes, and not because Stanisic was acting criminally in general, but "due to the unit's involvement in prior operations in Croatia wherein similar crimes were committed" and because operations in Croatia were similar to operations in Bosnia. Concerning Doboj, because the Chamber found that the accused must have known that the unit members had committed crimes earlier in Bosanski Samac, and in that awareness he organised the unit's involvement in the Doboj operations and that Stanisic was in contact with Karadzic, he must have known that setting up a unit, financing it, and loaning it to the operations in Doboj would result in them committing crimes and that his organising of the unit's involvement in those crimes -- organising the unit's involvement would assist those crimes. The appellant's resembling is truly extraordinary. The logic in relation to Bosanski Samac and Doboj really stretches the principle of culpability to breaking point. They are seeking to establish a culpable link to crimes in Bosanski Samac. Not through links to the crimes in Bosanski Samac but by links to crimes thousands of kilometres away, not by members of the unit but by other people. It is the most tenuous link and not one, of course, that a reasonable Trial Chamber would have relied upon. In relation to the Doboj, anyone, according to the appellant's logic, anyone who sets up a unit during the war, and some members of that unit commit crimes, not enough to send other members of that unit to the next operation rather than those who'd been acting criminally, you must disband the unit. Because if the unit goes on to commit crimes somewhere else, you're guilty of aiding and abetting, and then the appellant wants to talk about the reputation of the Tribunal and the reputation of this jurisprudence. Really? A few members of a unit commit crimes, the unit can no longer operate without an automatic inference of substantial effect. Now, finally, step 4 of the appellant's methodology. Having taken the findings they like, disregarded the remainder, and reassembled them anew, the appellant concludes their argument by seeking to avoid much of the evidence in Defence arguments. At paragraph 107, they fall back on their prevailing presumption of guilt. Stanisic and Simatovic "created, deployed, trained, financed, supplied," so on and so forth, "men and groups, knowing that they participated in one massive systemic campaign of violence against non-Serbs." It is this presumption of guilt that everything was one massive systemic campaign against non-Serbs, which leads them, at paragraph 83 and 84 of the reply, to say: "Had the Chamber considered Stanisic's and Simatovic's interaction with the perpetrator groups, it would have found that they were proximate to the crimes." Despite the fact that interactions were always in pursuant of lawful means, apparently consistent interaction in pursuit of lawful means makes it more likely that you'll commit crime in the future. So, to conclude, no reasonable trier of fact could have reached the conclusions that the appellant now urges upon this Chamber. The appellant fails to address the numerous findings by the Trial Chamber and the numerous findings by the majority, that there was more than a systemic campaign of criminal conduct. As found by the Chamber and consistently disregarded by the appellants, many of the operations were entirely legitimate. Many of the operations, unfortunately, were criminal. Many of the operations were a mixture of the two. But we cannot whitewash these detailed, consistent findings simply because the appellant wants to link the accused to a JCE. If I could have one more minute, Your Honour. In other words, the majority's findings that crime was not an inherent component of the operations must be confronted by the appellant. The fact that the unit behaved in furtherance of military objectives must be confronted by the appellant. The unit's propensity to act lawfully over five years despite others behaving criminally has to be confronted by the appellants. Where do we end up? Well, we heard before the lunch break the Prosecution say, you, the Appeals Chamber, can engage in the fact-findings to overturn these acquittals, and this is what they said: "Essentially the same process is here. This is a case about looking at the acts and the statements of the accused and the proper context of the prevailing ethnic campaign. Your Honours look at the pattern of crimes across the three regions, look at what the accused knew, look at with who they worked closely over a period of four years, look at what they did and what they did not do." How is that different to what this Trial Chamber did? It's exactly the same as what the Trial Chamber did. The Prosecution's appeal only gets home if you start with this approach: (1) there was only a criminal purpose. Nothing else was going on; (2) the accused knew of that JCE and that common purpose and nothing else; (3) that he contributed consistently to that criminal purpose and nothing else. And in order to get there, you have to remove hundreds of factual findings, ignore two years of trial advocacy, and hundreds of decisions by the majority. In our submission, the appeals should be dismissed. Thank you.

utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. We will now break for 20 minutes and resume for the response of counsel for Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We resume the hearing. Before giving the floor to counsel for Mr. Simatovic, may I inquire with the Prosecution if they need the break before their reply or if we can proceed after the response of counsel for Mr. Simatovic, directly to the reply?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be our preference to take the break after the response from Mr. Simatovic, if that pleases you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now we defer to counsel for Mr. Simatovic. You have the floor for one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, first, at the very outset, I wish to say the Defence for Franko Simatovic finds the Prosecution appeal brief to be unfounded in its entirety. The Defence believes that the conclusion of the Trial Chamber to acquit Simatovic on all counts of the indictment was well-founded and lawful. Any other position on the role, position, and responsibility of Franko Simatovic for the events he was charged with would be unfounded and unlawful. Defence would particularly like to point out that it stands fully by its response to the Prosecution appeal brief submitted on the 5th of November, 2013, as well as by all the factual and legal position provided during the proceedings. Detailed explanations in terms of why the judgement should be upheld were provided in our response to the Prosecution appeal brief, and we will do our utmost not to repeat those. However, first of all, Defence would like to make some introductory remarks. Although Simatovic was acquitted on all counts of the indictment, there is a number of findings made by the Trial Chamber on certain individual elements of criminal responsibility of the accused the Defence disagrees with and that it would have contested those had Franko Simatovic been convicted. Since the Trial Chamber in its final conclusion reached a correct and fair judgement, Defence is not in a position to contest the legal and factual findings it disagrees with. Out of an abundance of caution, Defence would like to point out that should the Appeals Chamber choose to accept any part of the Prosecution appeal, Simatovic may find himself in a position where his right to a fair trial and to a just trial, as well as to a two-instance procedure, would be substantially limited and in some aspects completely denied. Should the Appeals Chamber find the Prosecution's appeal to be grounded, partially or in entirety, and we believe the Appeals Chamber will not find it to be founded on any ground, the only decision the Appeals Chamber could render would be to return the case to a special Bench of the Tribunal for reconsideration with the application of the appropriate legal standard. This would be the only way to protect the accused Simatovic's right to a fair trial and his right to a two-instance procedure, because only then, in case the new judgement were a convicting one, would Simatovic have the possibility of filing an appeal against the findings he believes to be unfounded. The Prosecution, in its first ground of appeal, calls for an intervention by the Appeals Chamber to change or correct the applied legal standard in terms of participation in the JCE. In the second ground of appeal, although it is not explicitly stated in the appeal brief, the Prosecution ask that the Appeals Chamber apply a completely different law, to substitute the law or jurisprudence of specific direction under which Simatovic was tried with a law or jurisprudence established after the Simatovic judgement and after his acquittal. The Prosecution based its request on the legal basis established in some parts of the first-instance judgement. The situation on hand is particularly sensitive in that regard and significantly different from all other situations where the Appeals Chamber discussed whether there are any limitations imposed on its right to substitute a judgement of acquittal with a finding of guilt. At least two circumstances of particular importance. There isn't a single case where the accused was acquitted by the Trial Chamber on all counts and then convicted by the Appeals Chamber on some or all grounds of appeal by the Prosecution. Secondly, there isn't a single case where the accused who was acquitted by the Trial Chamber on all counts of the indictment was subsequently sentenced only because the law or jurisprudence relied upon here were changed. If the Appeals Chamber were to apply the jurisprudence from the Sainovic et al. appeal decision regarding specific direction, it would be a unique case where someone who was acquitted on the basis of the Appeals Chamber position was sentenced on the basis of the position by the same Appeals Chamber in a different composition. This case does not involve a discussion if the Appeals Chamber in the case of someone who had previously been convicted would rely on the same facts or whether the Appeals Chamber, on the basis of the same facts, could reach an acquittal on another count of the indictment that would have no or only a small impact on the overall sentence. It would entail a precedent where the accused would, if I may say so, be the victims of a legal theoretical discussion. That discussion is important in the sense of legal theory. It is important for the future of international law. But Franko Simatovic must not be the victim of that discussion. In this particular situation, which is significantly different from all other situations where this dilemma was placed before the Appeals Chamber in earlier proceedings, the position of the Defence is that should the Appeals Chamber choose not to uphold the Trial Chamber decision in its entirety, and it certainly should do so, or if as a last resort it decides not to return the case to the Trial Chamber for a reconsideration, it is evident that a serious violation of the fundamental principle of a fair trial would occur as recognised by international law as well as by many national legal systems. The international convention on civil and political rights as the fundamental legal authority in Article 14(5) states that anyone convicted of a crime has the right to have his or her conviction reconsidered by a court of higher instance in keeping with the law. In the UN Secretary-General report when, establishing the international Tribunal in paragraph 116, it is stated that the right to appeal is a fundamental element of individual, civil and political rights as established by the international convention on civil and political rights. If the Appeals Chamber were to adopt any grounds of appeal by the Prosecution, for which Defence is deeply convinced there is no reason to do, the only path to choose is that a new Trial Chamber is appointed, and if there is a conviction, any potential appeal should be considered by the Appeals Chamber. If the Appeals Chamber is to adopt any Prosecution grounds of appeal and if there is a dilemma in terms of how to proceed, this dilemma must be resolved to the benefit of the accused. If the Appeals Chamber has a dilemma in the context of different legitimate legal interests that may exist in this matter, the dilemma must be resolved to the benefit of the accused, Stanisic and Simatovic. As already mentioned, even the Prosecution alternatively requests for grounds 1 and 2 that the Appeals Chamber appoint a special Bench of the Tribunal which would apply the legal standard. This Defence believes that the understanding of specific direction as provided for in the trial judgement considered here and the Perisic appeal judgement is fully correct and based on best practice of international courts, which is something that is discussed in detail in our brief; hence, I will not return to it today. As regards ground 1 of the Prosecution appeal brief, the Prosecutor contends that the Trial Chamber committed an error in failing to find that Simatovic shared the intent to further the common criminal purpose of the JCE. The aforesaid error occurred by failing to provide a reasoned opinion on elements of JCE liability by applying an erroneous legal standard and erring in fact by sharing that Simatovic did not share the common criminal purpose of the JCE. The Prosecutor in its appeal states that the Trial Chamber acquitted Simatovic as a member of a JCE because he did not share the intent to achieve the common purpose without establishing whether the JCE existed or not. The Prosecutor is of the view that, first, it should be ascertained whether there are physical elements of the JCE in existence, and only then to establish if the accused possessed the mental element required. Defence points out that there is no rule in terms of which sequence is to be followed to establish the elements of the JCE. Defence states that the Trial Chamber, by thorough analysis, established that Simatovic did not possess the mental element for JCE. If the Trial Chamber concluded that intent necessary for JCE does not exist, there is no single legal reason for the Trial Chamber to continue establishing whether all or only some physical elements of the JCE existed or not. It is clear that in a situation where no mental element exists an acquittal is the only possible outcome. Defence also states that the Trial Chamber considered all elements necessary to establish the existence of the JCE alleged in the indictment. The Trial Chamber considered the entire crime base, all armed formations, and the relationship of the accused with those formations. The analysis conducted by the Trial Chamber did not result in a conclusion that there was a JCE in which Simatovic participated. Whether a JCE existed with regard to the same or similar factual situation and with the participation of some other persons is beyond the scope of the Trial Chamber, and it was under no obligation to express its position on that matter. It is worth noting that the position of the Prosecution is that the Trial Chamber erred for not analysing an important aspect of the JCE; the issue of creation of Greater Serbia. To discuss the issue of Greater Serbia as regards Simatovic, who at the time relevant to the indictment, was an employee of the Serbian DB of a lower rank without any possibility to influence the political or historical goals of the political or military leadership is pointless and without meaning. The Prosecution particularly objects the Trial Chamber not taking into account all evidence it deemed significant, although there is no dispute about the position that the Trial Chamber need not refer to each and every exhibit in the case file. The Prosecution particularly objects to the fact that the 45 exhibits provided for in Annex B were not cited by the Trial Chamber, although in their understanding they were obviously significant and relevant. This approach is clearly unfounded because of the very fact that of the 45 particularly relevant exhibits, not even the Prosecution themselves mentioned 13 of those in their final brief. The Defence concluded that the Trial Chamber acted correctly and concluded correctly by establishing that Simatovic did not possess the mental element necessary to participate in the JCE and that it analysed all other elements of importance for the existence of the JCE. It explains it appropriately, making the subground 1(A) of the Prosecution unfounded, and the Appeals Chamber should reject it in entirety. As regards subground 1(B), the Prosecutor states that the Trial Chamber applied an erroneous standard in assessing the evidence, especially in the discussion on the mens rea of the accused, and that they based their conclusions on fragments rather than the entirety of all exhibits. As already stated, the Trial Chamber does not have to take a position individually on each and every one of the 3.226 exhibits involved. That would be impossible, legally and technically. As regards mens rea for Simatovic, every question related to Simatovic's mens rea was looked at, and the brief refers to that. The Prosecutor, in their brief, try to prove Simatovic's intent through allegations concerning what happened in Lovinac, participation in the Vukovar operation, and the Udar operation. Each and every one of these assertions proffered by the Prosecutors themselves were looked into, as were others that the Prosecutor does not indicate in the final brief. And irrespective of all of that, the final conclusion of the Trial Chamber in relation to Simatovic is that there is no mens rea for JCE. The Trial Chamber analyses and uses the same logical and methodological approach in relation to all of Simatovic's activities and establishes that not a single one of these activities, individually or all together, meets the required standard for a conviction. The Defence wishes to say that although subground 1(B) pertains to both accused persons, not a single argument presented by the Prosecution pertains to Simatovic, and therefore it should be dismissed. Everything that is stated by the Prosecutor in this subground is an effort to impose a different interpretation of the evidence with no reference to where there is an error on the part of the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution is just trying to substitute one interpretation with another one, so this is not an erroneous application of standards but, rather, their disagreement with conclusions, and the Prosecutor wishes to present this as an erroneous and fragmentary approach in assessing the evidence. In section (D) of the first ground of appeal, the Prosecution states that they wish to help the Appeals Chamber by recapitulating the evidence that was presented before the Trial Chamber. Section (D) goes beyond the Notice of Appeal provided by the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor within the first ground complains about the conclusion of the Trial Chamber in relation to omissions on the part of the Chamber in terms of establishing intent regarding JCE as well as the mental element of the responsibility of the accused. (D) is a mix of conclusions of the Trial Chamber, quotations of certain exhibits from the case, and conclusions of the Prosecution themselves, and they wish in this way to assist the Trial Chamber in correcting the legal error that was made by the Trial Chamber. In this section there are - section (D) - there is a number of important conclusions of the Trial Chamber that would be seriously challenged by the Defence if a conviction was the initial trial judgement. In addition to that, these allegations are nothing else but a re-presentation of the Prosecution case. First of all, the Defence believes that the Prosecutor, in referring to section (D), has blatantly overstepped their Notice of Appeal. Nowhere in the Notice of Appeal is there any basis for presenting what is contained in section (D). The Prosecution's first ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber committed an error of law and/or an error of fact in failing to find shared intent to further common criminal purpose of JCE. So this is a question of a mental element of responsibility. In section (D), however, the Prosecutor presents his own view of the conclusions of the Trial Chamber and their subsequent interpretation of the evidence in the case. All of this should be dismissed, all of section D, because the Prosecution wishes to re-establish their case without indicating where the Trial Chamber erred. The Defence wishes to point out that in this situation where the Prosecutor wishes to substitute their own assessments with those made by the Trial Chamber, that should be dismissed altogether, in accordance with relevant jurisprudence. There cannot be relitigation and also they cannot present their own case once again because they disagree with the findings of the Trial Chamber because that is simply not done. In relation to section (D), the Defence already provided certain positions in their reply, and we will not be repeating them here and now. As for 1(C), the Defence believes that the Trial Chamber did not err, factually, when establishing that Simatovic did not share intent regarding JCE. The OTP suggests that the Trial Chamber erred in fact in finding that Stanisic and Simatovic did not share the intent to further the common criminal purpose of forcibly and permanently removing the majority of non-Serbs from large areas of the territory of Bosnia and Croatia. The Prosecution contends that Stanisic and Simatovic created, deployed, trained, financed, supplied, and supported multiple armed groups and continued supporting them knowing that they participated in one massive systemic campaign of violence against the non-Serb population. Obviously, this kind of general position taken by the Prosecution is not based on the evidence adduced at all. The Prosecution is asking the Appeals Chamber to do that, believing that the Trial Chamber omitted to do so. However, the entire appeal of the Prosecution looked at as a whole, and especially as regarding the accused Simatovic, links this accused person with certain things that happened allegedly in 1991 in Lovinac, then 1992 in Bosanski Samac and Doboj, and 1995 in Sanski Most. In addition to that, the Prosecution points out that Simatovic had contact only with one alleged member of the JCE, Milan Martic, namely, and in 1991 at that. So it is clear that the Prosecution is also aware of the fact that there is no evidence of Simatovic's alleged criminal activity and, nevertheless, they say that the Trial Chamber erred in viewing the evidence in its entirety. Even if one looks at the evidence in this way, it is obvious that even if viewed this way, this does not support the Prosecution's position about Simatovic's responsibility. Further on, the Prosecution states in blanket fashion the alleged things done by Simatovic, that he allegedly participated in a massive systemic campaign against non-Serbs. The Prosecution says that Simatovic created many armed groups, and they're not saying specifically which groups these were and how that was done, and there is no evidence that Simatovic created any such groups. The Prosecution also says that Simatovic deployed many armed groups, again without any specific statement as to which groups these are and where it was that Simatovic deployed them. Also, the Prosecution says, without basing this on any kind of evidence, that Simatovic trained armed groups, and they neglect the fact that the Trial Chamber, on the basis of material evidence, undeniable material evidence, establishes that Simatovic throughout this time that is relevant to the indictment was an intelligence man in the 2nd Intelligence Administration and not a military or police instructor. Further on, the Prosecution states without any grounds that Simatovic financed many armed groups. It is not clear that Simatovic had any capacity to finance anyone. It is particularly unclear whether the Prosecution is suggesting that Simatovic finance these groups from his own resources or the resources of the SDB of Serbia. It is quite clear that for -- either Simatovic did not have the capacity or position to do that, and therefore this is nonsense as regards the position of the Prosecution. Simatovic, in terms of his position and in terms of the office he held in the hierarchy of the SDB of Serbia, did not have the capacity to finance anyone. What the Defence said with regard to financing also goes for supplies and support to various armed groups. As for the relationship between the accused Simatovic and the alleged participant in the JCE, Milan Martic, the Defence does not wish to go into a discussion now regarding Martic's criminal intent but is convinced that the Prosecution did not give any evidence whatsoever that would indicate beyond a reasonable doubt that Simatovic shared this intent with Martic. Simatovic was in Knin briefly in 1991 at the time when crimes referred to in the indictment were not even committed and at the time when there was sporadic military operations undertaken with a view to maintaining control in the area and defending the areas from the Croatian armed forces. Therefore, it is absolutely unclear what kind of evidence was adduced during the proceedings that shows that Simatovic shared Martic's alleged intent to deport non-Serbs from the area of the SAO Krajina, especially when bearing in mind that the population, due to the military operations that were carried out by the JNA, were moving to areas where there were no such military operations. In a situation where there is a fluctuation of the population from an area of combat activity to other peaceful areas, one clearly has to delineate the two and establish what the evidence is that would lead to a finding that Simatovic knew of any kind of intent to expel the non-Serb population and that he shared this intent with Martic. There is simply no such evidence in this case. The reasons that the Prosecution tried to provide in their appeal in this regard are unfounded, illogical, and not based on the evidence adduced in this case. The Prosecution claims that Simatovic closely co-operated with Martic, and they refer to the trial judgement. The Defence, however, wishes to note that the Prosecution ignores the fact that the Trial Chamber clearly indicated that there is no evidence that Martic discussed his intention to deport non-Serbs with the accused. Also, there -- in the paragraph that is mentioned by the Prosecution, there is no mention of the accused Simatovic. Therefore, the Trial Chamber does not establish any close co-operation between Martic and Simatovic. It is only Stanisic's co-operation that is referred to. Obviously, there is no evidence to claim that there was close co-operation between Simatovic and Martic.
