utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The assertion by the Prosecution about the existence of a continuous relationship between the accused and Arkan and his SDG, starting with 1991 until 1995, is particularly unfounded. There is no proof of that and it seems that the Prosecution themselves are not certain about the existence of any kind of relationship between Simatovic and Arkan before 1995. We've already said that we disagree with some findings of the Trial Chamber, and one of the most conspicuous findings is the alleged participation of Simatovic in the deployment of Arkan and the SDG in 1995 in Treskavica. In our response to the appeal, we have elaborated this question in detail, pointing out the exhibit which undoubtedly shows that during the time of the operation, Simatovic was not in the area of the former Yugoslavia at all but in Greece. There is also no evidence which would prove beyond reasonable doubt that Simatovic participated or had a role in the deployment of Arkan and the SDG in Sanski Most in 1995. As regards the ground of appeal number 2, it is basically an assertion that the Trial Chamber erred in law by finding that it is necessary to establish that the acts of a person aiding and abetting be specifically directed so as to assist in the commission of crimes; in this specific case, the crimes in Bosanski Samac, Doboj, and the SAO Krajina. As regards subground 2(A), Defence explained its position in detail in its response. We stated why we believe that the condition of specific direction, as provided in the judgement, is based on the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and other international courts. Defence believes that there is no reason why this Appeals Chamber should confirm the position that -- it should not confirm the position taken by the Appeals Chamber in the same matter in the Perisic case. The Defence wishes to express its position further in case the Appeals Chamber finds that the Perisic finding was inadequate. Defence has an important remark to make as a matter of principle when it comes to the issue of specific direction. In the decision of the Appeals Chamber on the appeal in sentencing in the case of Dragan Nikolic, it was stated that the principle of applying the less stringent law, lex mitior, can be applied with regard to potential changes of the Statute of the international Tribunal which, in that specific case of Dragan Nikolic, referred to the type and duration of sentence that can be pronounced. The relevant criminal law relied on by this international Tribunal is the Statute of the international Tribunal. Since the Statute provides for only some basic characteristics of crimes in only four articles, and in one article it defines the type of responsibility, the jurisprudence of this international Tribunal defining the acts and types of responsibility basically present the relevant criminal code as it is understood in the countries of continental legal systems. If the jurisprudence changed, if I may say if the criminal law changed in the course of the proceedings, then according to the lex mitior principle, in the case of Simatovic, the most favourable legal regulation must be applied. If in the course of proceedings against Simatovic there are two interpretations of specific direction, if the two interpretations are of the same legal bearing, which is the case because they were both reached by the same Appeals Chamber, then in the case of Simatovic, the more favourable interpretation must be applied as provided for in the trial judgement. Defence would only briefly like to refer to the position of the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights in the case Scoppola versus Italy where, in paragraph 109, the court confirms the principle that in cases where there are differences in criminal codes at the time when the crime was committed and in subsequent criminal laws enforced before the final judgement, courts must apply the law whose provisions are the most favourable for the accused. Finally, in the Rome Statute of the ICC, in Article 24(2) states that should the law be changed before the final judgement, the more favourable law shall be applied. As regards the second ground of appeal under (B) and the third ground of appeal of the Prosecution, Defence would wish to point out the following. The Prosecution assert that the Trial Chamber, additionally or alternatively, erred in fact with regard to the reasons from appeal subground 2(A) given the fact that in the view of the Prosecution no reasonable Trial Chamber would not find that Stanisic and Simatovic were not aiders and abettors of the crimes committed in the municipalities of Bosanski Samac and Doboj, as well as in the area of SAO Krajina, even in a situation where it would be accepted that the element of specific direction is a constituent element of actus reus for aiding and abetting. In addition, the Prosecution presents a position that no reasonable Trial Chamber would not find that the contribution of the accused to the crimes in Bosanski Samac and Doboj, as well as in the area of the SAO Krajina, are not specifically or directly directed at the commission of crimes. The Defence asserts that such position is unacceptable and unfounded and that the Trial Chamber correctly found that Simatovic is not responsible for aiding and abetting these crimes. Defence reiterates that if indirect evidence is used to establish a fact that a conviction would be based on, that conclusion must be the only reasonable conclusion that could be reached on the basis of such indirect evidence. If the evidence can be used to reach more than one reasonable conclusion, the accused may not be pronounced guilty and the Trial Chamber correctly applied it. As regards the events in Bosanski Samac municipality, the Defence presented much evidence which undoubtedly shows that the municipality of Bosanski Samac was organised as a new municipality with the aim of organising the Serbian people in the area for defence under the leadership of the Bosanski Samac SDS. In the area, the dominant defence role was played by the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA, which was well armed with heavy and light weaponry. The leadership of Bosanski Samac established direct contacts with the command of the Yugoslav airforce in Belgrade; specifically, with General Bajic. It is obvious, therefore, that under such circumstances prevailing in the new municipality of Bosanski Samac, a simple operative of the intelligence administration of the SDB sitting in his office in Belgrade cannot have any influence over the events in Bosanski Samac, let alone to direct or channel those events in any way. The only reasonable conclusion is that Franko Simatovic lacked the capacity and authority, nor was he factually present, and that it could not be concluded that he aided or abetted the events in Bosanski Samac in the time relevant for the proceedings. As regards Doboj, it is the Prosecution's obvious intent to establish a link between the events in Doboj and the unit of the DB of Republika Srbija via Radojica Bozovic. Ample evidence was led during the proceedings that undoubtedly shows that Radojica Bozovic was a member of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time relevant for the indictment. In documents of the Serbian Republic of BiH MUP for April and May 1992, Bozovic was designated as a member of the ministry and received his salary from the ministry. Other evidence confirms that as well. The training of special units at Ozren was commanded by a certain Slobodan Katanic, a member of the BiH MUP. The crime in Doboj, as charged in the indictment, happened on the 12th of July, 1992, and it is obvious from the evidence that was led that Bozovic could not have participated; namely, between the 26th of June and the 23rd of July, he was hospitalised in the general hospital in Doboj after being wounded. Following his release and recovery, he was assigned to other tasks and duties. Since Radojica Bozovic is the only link with the accused, and bearing in mind that the Prosecution draws that connection to find any involvement in the crimes of Doboj, bearing all of this in mind, the only reasonable conclusion is the one reached by the Trial Chamber, which is that Franko Simatovic has nothing to do with the events and crimes in Doboj. Furthermore, the Prosecution instructs the Appeals Chamber that the Trial Chamber found that the TO and the police of the SAO Krajina committed murders, deportations, and persecution of non-Serb civilians in the SAO Krajina between April 1991 and 1994. Although the Trial Chamber established that indeed there were certain links between the accused and groups, such as the SAO Krajina police and TO, the Trial Chamber nevertheless correctly found that these links and evidence indicating the existence of those links are insufficient to conclude that the accused, including Franko Simatovic, aided and abetted the crimes committed by the SAO Krajina police and TO. The Trial Chamber explicitly established that certain links between Franko Simatovic and certain groups in the Krajina are not sufficient in themselves to impose as the only reasonable conclusion that Simatovic aided and abetted the crimes committed by these groups, if any. If all the findings of the Trial Chamber that the Defence does not fully agree with were absolutely correct, again there would be an alternative explanation of what Simatovic did, and that is what the Trial Chamber found; namely, that there were connections that were established and directed towards supporting the war effort of the Serbs in SAO Krajina, rather, the effort to control territory. Not to help in the commission of any kind of crime. So let us simplify matters. Although we do not agree with certain factual findings of the Trial Chamber in this section either, again, even if that were absolutely correct, it would be unreasonable to establish that these connections happened in order for crimes to be committed rather than having another objective involved. The Prosecution, during the proceedings, had to proffer evidence that Simatovic's activity in Krajina, in a very limited period of time, from April 1991 until August 1991, was exclusively geared towards aiding and abetting the commission of crimes charged in the indictment. Since there is no such evidence, what suits the Prosecution the most is to have the broadest possible test of responsibility for aiding and abetting. Simatovic was indeed in Knin in the period of two and a half months between May 1991 and August 1991, but we have not said that his activity was not geared towards aiding and abetting the commission of any crimes and that it is equally important to mention that in that period, when Simatovic was in Knin, crimes were not committed, and he could not have known of any crimes. The evidence clearly shows that Milan Martic, already in 1990, organised the police of - milicija - the SAO Krajina and reached a decision on its financing and training. There is evidence that until December 1990, this police was financed from Zagreb and later companies from the area of SAO Krajina. Martic decided on the allocation of funds, and there were donations from Germany as well. There is a great deal of evidence about this. Also, to the effect that the Ministry of Defence of Republic of Serbia financed the TO of the SAO Krajina through the public accounting service in Knin and commercial banks. All agreements on financing were agreed at top level between the government of the SAO Krajina and Slobodan Milosevic or the minister of the interior, Zoran Sokolovic, and there is also material evidence to that effect. Simatovic had no contact whatsoever with top state officials. He is considerably below these persons in the state hierarchy. Simatovic does not belong to the circle of persons who discuss matters and reached decisions regarding state policy in any aspect, financing included. Simply, he did not have that kind of authority within his service, the DB of Serbia, let alone at some higher level. The position that Simatovic held rules out any kind of allocation of financial resources that could finance the forces of the Serbs in the SAO Krajina. The Prosecution points out that Simatovic personally participated in certain operations where Martic acted with the intention of committing crimes. There is a reference to Lovinac there. The Defence wishes to state on this occasion as well that Simatovic had nothing whatsoever to do with the attack against Lovinac, which was in the immediate vicinity of the largest arms depot of the JNA in the area of Lika. This depot was blocked by the Croatian forces, so it was only the JNA that made the decision to break through this blockade. The forces of the Knin Corps did carry out this breakthrough, and with regard to this operation, Mladic took notes about this in his diary, and that is in evidence. As a result of the war rations concerning the deblockade of the arms depot, the population of Lovinac left the area. In Mladic's diary, which is material in this case, there is no mention of Simatovic, and therefore it is only reasonable to conclude that this attack was planned and carried out by the JNA. The Defence also contends that Simatovic had absolutely nothing to do with the activities in Glina and Struga in the summer of 1991. We just need to briefly say a few words about the alleged contribution of Simatovic to the alleged JCE in Sanski Most. The Prosecution contends that the evidence indicates that the accused financed and deployed Arkan in Sanski Most in 1990 and 1995. The Prosecution also contends that between 1991 and 1993, the Serb Volunteer Guard and Arkan committed many crimes against non-Serb civilians in the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, Bijeljina, and Zvornik, with the assistance of the SDB of Serbia, which is something that the accused would have to know about. We would like to point out that this is contradictory and quite unclear as far as the appeal is concerned. Namely, the Prosecution does not say that the Franko Simatovic was not responsible with regard to what the SDG did before 1995 in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, Bijeljina, and Zvornik, before 1995, but they want Simatovic to be held accountable for aiding and abetting crimes in Sanski Most because, allegedly, Stanisic knew about this previously, and he had to know that the SDG could commit the crimes of persecution and murder. To this day, the Defence does not understand how come Simatovic, and on the basis of somebody else's knowledge about crimes committed previously, there could have been an awareness that such crimes could be committed yet again. There is no evidence linking Simatovic to what happened in Sanski Most, except for the testimony of an absolutely incredible witness, a witness that totally lacks credibility, and we have already dealt with this extensively in our brief. Arkan and SDG were sent to Banja Luka as members of the RSK under the direct control of the 11th Corps. Witness Pejlovic, Arkan's first deputy in the SDG, testified before the Trial Chamber and confirmed all of this material evidence is absolutely correct. In addition to that, Arkan came to the area of Sanski Most as invited by the top leadership of Republika Srpska and agreement with the officials of the army of the RSK and placed himself under the direct control of General Talic, who was then commander of the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS and who commanded the entire defence of Banja Luka and Sanski Most. In this context, when the Defence, on the one hand, weighs all the adduced evidence and, on the other hand, the position and title that Simatovic had in the SDB, it is absolutely not clear on the basis of which evidence the Prosecution contends that Simatovic had the capacity at all to organise salaries and medical care for members of the SDG. The same pertains to Operation Pauk, Spider, where it is claimed that Simatovic, together with Stanisic, made it possible for the SDG to take part in this operation. The Prosecution mentions Simatovic, although Simatovic did not participate in any preparatory meeting for this operation with high officials, including Mladic, Perisic, and others. It is clear that Simatovic did not have any capacity to make it possible to have the SDG participate in Operation Pauk. Also, there is no evidence in this case that Simatovic provided ammunition and uniforms to the SDG in view of the specific position that Simatovic had in the service. The Defence wishes to conclude at this point that there was ample evidence that proved beyond a reasonable doubt that Simatovic, in terms of his position and in terms of the title he had and in terms of his job description, could not have proposed, let alone approved or secured financial support to anyone, the SDG included. The Defence wishes finally to conclude that the Trial Chamber should fully affirm the trial judgement that all three grounds of appeal of the Prosecution should be dismissed and kindly ask this Appeals Chamber to affirm the acquittal pronounced for Franko Simatovic because that is the only judgement that is possible in terms of fact and law. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We resume the hearing, and I will give the floor to the Prosecution for their reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and Your Honours. I have just four points in reply, and I will endeavour to be brief. The first point relates to the submission made by counsel for Mr. Stanisic that the Prosecution, through its appeal, is seeking to construct a new house without looking at whether the existing doors and windows are valid. We accept that the doors and the windows in the house constructed by the Chamber are sound. Our problem is that the Chamber constructed its house without any foundations, and the missing foundations, of course, are the common criminal purpose analysis and the analysis of the accused's knowledge of that common criminal purpose. Without those foundations, the house constructed by the Chamber cannot be sound. The Defence don't address these two issues in their submissions. We've not heard anything from them that will help us to understand where is the missing analysis in the judgement, where is the missing analysis on the common criminal purpose and on the accused's knowledge of that criminal purpose. The foundations of the house are still, indeed, missing. Your Honours, we accept, of course, that the Trial Chamber made many findings throughout the judgement that are sound. Other than the ones we challenge in ground 3 and the ones tainted by the absence of the common criminal purpose lens, we accept the findings in the judgement, as we've set out in brief and as we've argued in our submissions today. But what we want is for Your Honours to fix the missing foundations. To add those foundations into the house. And the fact that the rest of the structure of the house is sound supports our position that this case is not so difficult to fix. Counsel for Mr. Stanisic concluded his submissions by saying that the OTP can only succeed in its appeal if it establishes three things or if we accept that there was a criminal purpose where the crimes were inherent to the territorial control, if we accept that the accused knew of that, and we accept that the accused contributed consistently. We agree with those three propositions. But again, the problem is that despite all of the evidence adduced by the Prosecution at trial about the common criminal purpose, about the accused's knowledge of that, about their contributions, the Trial Chamber did not factor that into its analysis of shared intent. My second point concerns counsel for Mr. Stanisic's arguments that the Prosecution is asking Your Honours to assume guilt in this case. In relation to our bank robbery hypothetical, counsel has suggested that this demonstrates there is a presumption of guilt inherent in our argument, that we're asking you to suggest that a driver who indeed drove lawfully to the bank and others robbed it afterwards should be guilty. But, of course, this misses the key point of the hypothetical example: It's about the relevance of the missing common criminal purpose analysis in determining intent and why it was not open to the Trial Chamber to simply fail to address it all together in its analysis. Your Honours, I want to clarify that we, of course, do not say that you should assume the common criminal purpose or assume that the accused knew about it. In Mr. Marcussen's submissions, he was dealing with a Defence argument raised in the briefing that perhaps one might view the Trial Chamber's approach as having assumed arguendo the common criminal purpose. Our point is that if you really look at that as a suggestion and follow that through, you can see from the Trial Chamber's own findings that it did not credit arguendo the common criminal purpose. And even if it had, Your Honours, that still would not have been a valid approach to adjudicating a JCE case. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber had to engage with the evidence the Prosecution produced about the common criminal purpose because that evidence has a bearing on the accused's connection to the common criminal purpose. For example, the evidence about the pattern of crimes, the evidence about the statements of the JCE members, Karadzic and others, who clearly expressed their intent to ethnically cleanse, that had to be factored into the evidentiary mix in order to understand what the accused, given their connections and relationships and co-ordination and co-operation with those JCE members, what they would have known and indeed did know. Your Honours, the third point concerns the Defence's attempts to trivialise what has happened in this case. Counsel for Mr. Stanisic has suggested that the Prosecution's position is so far reaching --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Afande would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AFANDE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. A while ago you talked about the foundation of the house. I believe you were referring to your first ground of appeal, which according to you - I stand to be corrected, of course - according to you, the Trial Chamber should have reached its conclusions on the basis of the common criminal purpose before analysing the mens rea element. Am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We say it was an integral part of that analysis. Whether the Chamber made a finding as step number 1 or whether it factored it into the intent analysis, the analysis had to be done as part of the adjudication of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AFANDE
utterances.text: Right. [Interpretation] But had that been the case, and the way that you present it is that there has been an error in law, what legal finding do you rely on, in other words, that you have not applied the law, or is there a case law which enables you to support this analysis which the Trial Chamber would not have made?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: We say it's an error of law, Your Honour, because it was a failure to provide a reasoned opinion, which is one category of legal error recognised in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. So whenever you fail to address an essential issue in the case or you fail to address essential evidence in the case, that can constitute a failure to provide a reasoned opinion and constitutes a legal error. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AFANDE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue? You seem to have given us two citations this morning - in Kvocka, paragraph 23, and Gotovina, paragraph 12, I believe - to illustrate your position which seems to not conform with your appeals brief. How can you explain this difference between your position of a reasoned opinion that is lacking and your initial position in your appeals brief which does not address the question of a reasoned opinion?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in ground 1 of our appeal, we have indeed alleged that the Trial Chamber has failed to provide a reasoned opinion. So the submissions made today are consistent with the arguments that we've made in our brief, and we have in the brief included additional citations to support that argument, but it certainly is the case that what we are maintaining today is an explanation of what we've already put in our brief. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AFANDE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my third point in reply concerns the Defence suggestion that the Prosecution is taking such a far-reaching position that we are suggesting any time a minor infraction is committed in the course of a conflict, a unit must be disbanded. Your Honours, of course that's not what is at issue here. Let's not forget what happened in Bosanski Samac and Doboj. In Bosanski Samac, the unit, the accused's unit that they directed and controlled, beat and killed non-Serb detainees after the take-over and throughout April 1992 and into May. The Chamber discussed evidence of the unit members beating detained non-Serbs on the back of their heads with a rubber truncheon, beating to death a 60-year-old man with a table leg before dragging him into a courtyard, shooting him, ordering others to throw "this dog into the Sava River," that's at paragraph 666, beating Muslims in the crotch, and stating that Muslims should not propagate. That's at paragraph 665, 666, 673, and 676. The Chamber accepted that unit members perpetrated these beatings and killings; paragraph 685. In addition, the Chamber found that on 7 May 1992, unit members massacred 16 civilians held within a warehouse; paragraph 608 to 615 and 685.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: In Doboj, knowing of these ongoing crimes in Bosanski Samac, the accused deployed another unit -- other unit members who were not busy still terrorising civilians in Bosanski Samac into the Doboj take-over on 3 May 1992. That's at paragraph 718 of the judgement. By 7 May 1992, they had caused thousands of Muslim and Croats to flee Doboj town. On 24 May 1992, unit members took ten detainees from a prison and they were not heard or seen of again. That's at paragraph 777. In June 1992, members of the unit killed at least 30 civilian detainees from a warehouse and buried them in mass graves; paragraph 776. In May or June 1992, unit members attacked the villages of Doboj municipality. They captured, tortured, and killed members of the Muslim and Croat armies and killed the whole civilian --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speaker is kindly asked to slow down for the purpose of interpretation into B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Of Johovac; paragraph 747. So, Your Honours, it really is a misrepresentation of the record to suggest that the accused would not have known about the massive and appalling nature of the crimes and the role that they played in the ethnic cleansing campaign. Your Honours, my fourth point, and I'm reluctant to tell you I actually have five points, a problem with my numbering, the fourth point concerns aiding and abetting. Counsel for Mr. Stanisic argued today that that not much turned on the Trial Chamber's legal error requiring specific direction as an element of aiding and abetting. But let's look at how the majority's error resulted in a misappreciation of the accused's role in aiding and abetting the crimes of the unit in Bosanski Samac and Doboj which included murders, forcible displacement, and persecution. Let's look at how this erroneous requirement, which has been found to be not consistent with customary international law, has resulted in their acquittal. In paragraph 2359, the Trial Chamber concluded that: "Contributions of the accused assisted the commission of the crimes." In other words, the Trial Chamber found that the legal requirement of contribution was met. In the subsequent paragraph, though, the majority considers that this assistance did not have a substantial effect because their acts were not specifically directed at the crimes. So, as a direct result, it acquitted the accused of aiding and abetting in relation to crimes in Bosanski Samac and Doboj. So, Your Honours, the suggestion that the specific direction requirement did not have an impact on the results achieved in this case is not accurate based on a reading of the Chamber's own findings. Your Honours, finally, the counsel for both accused have addressed the issue of the fairness of entering convictions on appeal. And we agree that that is a matter that Your Honours will obviously be concerned to think carefully about. But, Your Honours, this is a question that has already been addressed and decided by this Appeals Chamber. Over the years, the argument has been put many times that the Appeals Chamber should not enter convictions on appeal where there is no further right of appeal, but the Appeals Chamber has consistently taken the position that it does have that power and that it is appropriate to do so. Your Honours, this power, of course, stems from Article 25 of the Statute and the Chamber's power to affirm, reverse, or revise decisions of the Trial Chamber. And for examples of where the Appeals Chamber has entered convictions before, I refer you to the Djordjevic appeal judgement at paragraph 928, Popovic appeal judgement at paragraph 539, the Gatete appeal judgement of the ICTR Appeals Chamber, paragraph 265. And there are, of course, many additional examples over the years of the Tribunal's cases. Your Honours, it has already been determined that this is not inconsistent with the fair trial rights of the accused. And in particular, both the ICCPR and the European Court of Human Rights -- European Convention of Human Rights recognise either reservations or exceptions that this is not an absolute right to have an appeal from a conviction if the conviction is entered by the highest level Tribunal, and that is what the situation, of course, is here before Your Honours. So, Your Honours, we submit that this is a well-decided, already determined issue in terms of your power to enter convictions. That is beyond dispute. It is now for Your Honours to determine whether you want to exercise that power in the present case. For all of the reasons that I have given earlier in my submissions on remedy, we say that is the most appropriate submission, the most appropriate remedy in the circumstances of this case. Thank you, Your Honours. Oh, Your Honours, I would just mention that we have copies of the slides that we relied upon today which we will hand out for your legal officers and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. Is this concluding your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It concludes our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. So this also concludes the hearing of appeal in this case. Before we adjourn, let me just take a moment to thank the parties for their work on this case and for their arguments today. I would also like to express my gratitude to the Registry staff here in the courtroom who have facilitated our hearing today, and in particular the interpreters for their excellent assistance. Sometimes the interpreter missed it and because the counsel go too quickly their submissions, and I wish to thank them particularly. And, of course, I also thank the legal officers of the Appeals Chamber. The Appeals Chamber will render its decision in due course, and the parties will be notified. The proceedings are adjourned.
